sections.body: 7.1 Introduction (pp. 211-212). Static analysis methods are analytical methods that use geomaterial strength and compressibility properties to determine nominal geotechnical resistance and deformation. The chapter focuses on methods for the nominal geotechnical resistance of single piles and pile groups in axial compression, uplift and lateral loading, and the resulting vertical and lateral deformations. Important considerations: (1) static analysis methods are an integral part of the design process, needed to determine the most cost effective pile type and to estimate the number of piles and the required pile lengths; the designer must know the design loads and project performance criteria. (2) Many methods are available; those presented are relatively simple methods that have provided reasonable agreement with full scale field results, and many are in AASHTO (2014); more sophisticated methods may be used and in some cases give better results; whatever the method, experience from its past field performance should be applied continually. (3) Designers should fully understand the basis, limitations and applicability of a chosen method, particularly computer solutions whose assumptions may not be apparent, and a method should have proven agreement with full scale field results. (4) Evaluation and confirmation of pile drivability is an integral part of limit state design: designs with fewer, larger pile sections of greater nominal resistance are more frequently used, and the ability of these piles to reach the penetration depths needed for all resistance and deformation requirements is a critical design check; a drivability analysis combines this chapter's geotechnical aspects with the wave equation procedures of Chapter 12 and should be performed by the engineer during design. Construction procedures can significantly influence pile behavior: the methods lead to successful designs only with appropriate construction techniques and construction monitoring, which should be integral to design and construction, and static load tests, wave equation analysis or dynamic monitoring for construction control should, whenever possible, confirm a static design. The chapter covers background, static analysis for compression, uplift and lateral loads, pile group settlement, special design events, limited guidance for liquefaction susceptible soils (detailed seismic design is beyond the manual's scope and is in GEC-3, Kavazanjian et al. 2011), and construction issues pertinent to static analysis, using AASHTO (2014) notation and load and resistance factors. Subsections: 7.1.1 Static Analysis Methods in Limit State Design; 7.1.2 Events During and After Pile Driving; 7.1.3 Load Transfer; 7.1.4 Effective Stress; 7.1.5 Resistance Factors; 7.1.6 Interdiscipline Communication and Coordination.

subsections.title: Static Analysis Methods in Limit State Design
subsections.body: There are four general types of static analysis in this chapter (pp. 212-213). They determine: (1) the nominal resistance in axial compression of a pile or pile group - the long-term resistance, the resistance of layers subject to scour, liquefaction or downdrag or otherwise unsuitable for long-term support, the minimum pile penetration, pile lengths for bid quantities, the soil resistance at the time of driving (SRD) and the required nominal driving resistance Rndr; (2) the nominal resistance in axial tension, which in some cases also sets the minimum penetration; (3) the nominal lateral resistance and lateral deformation, by soil-structure interaction methods that also guide pile section selection; and (4) the settlement of a pile group under the structure's service loads. The factored resistance of a pile or pile group is the smaller of the factored geotechnical resistance of the surrounding soil or rock and the factored structural resistance of the pile(s). Vertical (settlement) and lateral deformation of pile groups are computed with factored loads at the service limit state. The static resistance along the shaft and at the toe can be estimated from laboratory shear strength parameters, in-situ test data (SPT, CPT), or geomaterial parameters back-analysed from performance data.
key_points: Four static analyses: axial compression, axial tension, lateral resistance and deformation, pile group settlement
Factored resistance = smaller of the factored geotechnical resistance and the factored structural resistance
Settlement and lateral deformation of groups use factored loads at the service limit state

subsections.title: Events During and After Pile Driving
subsections.body: The soil and weaker rock in which a pile is installed are almost always disturbed (p. 214). The degree of disturbance depends on the soil and rock type and density, the pile type (displacement or low-displacement) and the installation method (driven, vibrated, drilled, jetted); for driven piles substantial disturbance and remolding is unavoidable. Over the long term, scour, settlement, pore pressure fluctuations, seismic and other extreme events may occur, and are addressed in the strength, extreme event and service limit states so that the embedment and foundation stiffness are sufficient.

subsections.title: Cohesionless Soils
subsections.body: The resistance of piles driven into cohesionless soil depends primarily on the relative density of the soil (pp. 214-216). Driving increases the relative density of loose to medium dense soil close to the pile through vibration and lateral displacement, most of all next to displacement piles; Broms (1966) and later studies found the zone of densification extends 3 to 5.5 diameters from the pile shaft and 3 to 5 diameters below the pile toe (Figure 7-1). Large-displacement piles such as closed-end pipe and precast concrete piles densify cohesionless soil more than low-displacement open-end pipe or steel H-piles. In dense sands and gravels, negative pore pressures generated during driving can temporarily increase the resistance; as they dissipate the resistance decreases (relaxation), as the shear strength equation shows (Eq. 7-1). In saturated cohesionless silts and loose to medium dense fine sands, driving can generate high positive pore pressures that temporarily reduce the resistance; the gain with time (setup) is generally quicker than in clays because pore pressures dissipate faster.

subsections.title: Cohesive Soils
subsections.body: When piles are driven into saturated cohesive soil, the soil near the pile is disturbed and radially compressed (pp. 216-217). In soft or normally consolidated clays the zone of disturbance is generally within one pile diameter around the pile; in saturated stiff clays there are also changes in secondary structure (closing of fissures), remolding and loss of previous stress history effects next to the pile. Figure 7-2 (after Broms 1966) shows the disturbance zone and the heave that displacement piles can cause. The disturbance generates high excess positive pore pressures that temporarily reduce the shear strength, the nominal geotechnical resistance and the blow count; as the soil reconsolidates, the shear strength and resistance increase (setup), the opposite of relaxation. The zone and magnitude of disturbance depend on the soil sensitivity, the driving method and the pile geometry. Limited data for partially saturated cohesive soils indicate that driving does not generate high pore pressures, so significant setup does not occur.
figures: Figure 7-2: Disturbance of cohesive soils during pile driving (after Broms 1966)

subsections.title: Additional Soil Resistance Considerations
subsections.body: Many projects need more than one static analysis (pp. 217-219): one for the number and length of piles to support the structure loads, and a second for the resistance the pile will meet during installation, which sets the capability of the driving equipment and the minimum pile section for drivability. At a bridge pier subject to scour (Figure 7-3) the first analysis neglects the soil in the scour zone, which may not be available for long-term support, and the second includes it because it resists driving; piles driven through loose uncompacted fill (Figure 7-4) are treated the same way. The resistance computed in the scourable or unsuitable layer is added to the required nominal resistance to give the required nominal driving resistance. The plans should give the controlling factored load, the nominal resistance, the required nominal driving resistance and the minimum penetration depth: in the manual's example 420 kips of soil resistance must be overcome to reach the minimum penetration for a 300-kip nominal resistance in compression, and specifying only the 300 kips could be misinterpreted and lead to claims (driving criteria: Chapter 17).

subsections.title: Load Transfer
subsections.body: The nominal resistance Rn of a pile in homogeneous soil is the sum of the shaft resistance Rs and the toe resistance Rp (Eq. 7-2, p. 219). The equation assumes the pile toe and shaft have both moved enough relative to the adjacent soil to develop the nominal shaft and toe resistances at the same time; generally the displacement needed to mobilize the shaft resistance is smaller than that needed for the toe. This approach has been used for all piles except very large piles, more than 36 inches in diameter or width. Figure 7-5 shows typical load transfer profiles, as obtained from a static load test with strain gages or telltales along the shaft: (a) no shaft resistance, the full head load reaching the toe; (b) uniform shaft resistance, typical of cohesive soil; (c) triangular shaft resistance, typical of cohesionless soil.
equations: Eq. 7-2: Rn = Rs + Rp
figures: Figure 7-5: Typical load transfer profiles

subsections.title: Effective Stress
subsections.body: The vertical effective stress at a depth is the total vertical stress from the weight of the overlying soil minus the pore water pressure there (pp. 221-222). An Effective Stress Diagram plots it against depth and is used in many static resistance and settlement calculations. It needs the total unit weight and thickness of each layer (from the boring logs, density tests on undisturbed cohesive samples, or SPT N values with the visual classification) and the depth of the water table; the total vertical stress is summed layer by layer (Section 5.2.2) and the pore pressure is the unit weight of water (62.4 lb/ft3) times the height of water. The design water table should be compared with the levels found in the subsurface exploration and allow for seasonal variation. Figures 7-6 and 7-7 are examples with the water table below and above the ground surface.

subsections.title: Resistance Factors
subsections.body: Resistance factors for driven pile design are in AASHTO (2014) Table 10.6.5.2.3-1 (pp. 223-226). A resistance factor is a statistically based multiplier on the nominal resistance from a specific analysis method, tied with the load factors to a target reliability index beta; it is not a direct replacement for an allowable stress design factor of safety. With a static analysis the factored resistance Rr is at most the shaft resistance times the shaft method's resistance factor plus the toe resistance times the toe method's factor (Eq. 7-3), with Rs = fs As and Rp = qp Ap (Eqs. 7-4, 7-5). Table 7-1 gives the static analysis factors: compression - alpha-method 0.35, Schmertmann (1975) 0.50, Nordlund 0.45, the beta-method differing between AASHTO and the manual, Brown (2001), API RP2A and Eslami and Fellenius not in AASHTO; block failure in cohesive soil 0.60; tension - Nordlund 0.35, alpha 0.25, beta 0.20, lambda 0.30, SPT 0.25, CPT 0.40; group uplift 0.50; lateral 1.0. Where the nominal resistance is found by a static load test, dynamic testing, wave equation analysis or a dynamic formula, the field method's factor phi_dyn is used (Table 7-2): 0.80 for a static load test with dynamic testing, 0.75 for a static load test alone or dynamic testing of every production pile, 0.65 for dynamic testing of at least two piles per site condition and 2 % of production piles, 0.50 for the wave equation at end of drive, 0.40 for the FHWA Modified Gates formula, 0.10 for the Engineering News formula; in tension 0.60 for a static load test and 0.50 for dynamic testing with signal matching. For a small group (fewer than 3 piles per substructure unit in this manual) AASHTO recommends reducing the factors in Tables 7-1 and 7-2 by 20 %. The AASHTO calibration considered few large diameter pipe piles (Brown and Thompson 2015), which a designer of piles over 24 inches should consider.

subsections.title: Interdiscipline Communication and Coordination
subsections.body: Design and construction need clear communication among the structural, geotechnical, geologic, hydraulic and construction professionals (p. 227). Figure 2-3 in Chapter 2 gives the flow chart of the driven pile design and construction process with the main areas of coordination in LRFD design and construction, and Tables 2-4 and 2-5 detail what is communicated. Effective communication is essential to a cost-effective foundation that meets all the strength, extreme event and service limit state requirements.

sections.title: Strength Limit States
sections.summary: Geotechnical strength checks: axial compression and uplift of single piles and groups, bearing stratum punching, and drivability. Seven static methods for piles in soil (7.2.1.3): Nordlund, alpha, API RP2A, effective stress beta, Brown (SPT), Eslami and Fellenius (CPT), Nottingham and Schmertmann (CPT); piles in soft rock and to hard rock (7.2.1.4). FHWA recommends Nordlund for cohesionless soils, alpha for cohesive soils, and API for large diameter pipe piles. Also: group compression, tension, setup and relaxation, lateral resistance, length estimates, groundwater, dewatering, scour, downdrag.
sections.body: 7.2 Strength Limit States (p. 227). The strength limit state ensures local and global strength and stability against statistically significant load combinations occurring during the structure design life. Strength limit state design includes an evaluation of the nominal geotechnical and structural resistances, as well as the loss of lateral and vertical support in the design flood event due to scour. Geotechnical aspects of strength limit state design include: axial compression resistance of single piles; axial compression resistance of pile groups; uplift resistance of single piles; uplift resistance of pile groups; bearing stratum punching failure; and constructability, including drivability. Subsections: 7.2.1 Determination of Nominal Resistance for Single Piles; 7.2.2 Resistance of Pile Groups in Axial Compression; 7.2.3 Design for Axial Tension Resistance; 7.2.4 Nominal Axial Resistance Changes after Pile Driving; 7.2.5 Nominal Lateral Resistance; 7.2.6 Pile Length Estimates for Contract Documents; 7.2.7 Groundwater Effects and Buoyancy; 7.2.8 Site Dewatering; 7.2.9 Scour; 7.2.10 Downdrag.

Evaluates nominal geotechnical and structural resistances and the loss of support from design flood scour
Axial compression resistance of single piles and of pile groups

subsections.title: Determination of Nominal Resistance for Single Piles
subsections.body: Static analysis methods for the nominal axial resistance of a single driven pile (printed pp. 227-280): the general approach (7.2.1.1), an overview of the methods and when each applies (7.2.1.2), seven methods for piles in soil (7.2.1.3: Nordlund, alpha, P2A/API, effective stress beta, Brown, Eslami and Fellenius, Nottingham and Schmertmann), piles to soft and weak or hard rock (7.2.1.4), and software for the computations (7.2.1.5). The FHWA recommended methods are Nordlund in cohesionless soils, the alpha-method in cohesive soils and the API method for large diameter pipe piles.

subsections.title: General
subsections.body: Numerous static analysis methods are available for the nominal geotechnical resistance of a single pile (printed pp. 227-229). Section 7.2.1.3 details methods for piles in cohesionless, cohesive and layered profiles from SPT or laboratory data, and methods based on CPT results. A method should have proven agreement with full-scale field results in soil conditions like the project's, with the pile type and installation conditions (impact or vibratory driving) to be used, and some AASHTO resistance factors require specific procedures for the soil strength properties. A static analysis iteratively assumes a pile depth. Regional geology or construction control may justify local calibration of methods and resistance factors. Table 7-3 compares the methods in AASHTO (2014) with those in the manual: Meyerhof (1976, SPT) 0.30, Nordlund 0.45, alpha-method 0.35, beta-method (AASHTO) 0.25, lambda-method 0.40 and Schmertmann (1975, CPT) 0.50 have AASHTO resistance factors; API RP2A, Brown (2001) and Eslami and Fellenius (1997) have none; the manual's beta-method follows Fellenius (1991) and differs from AASHTO's.

subsections.title: Static Analysis Overview
subsections.body: Agencies often specify design methods based on experience; the methods in this chapter should be chosen by their applicability to the soil conditions, the pile type and the laboratory or in-situ data (printed pp. 229-232). Tables 7-4 and 7-5 give an overview of methods for cohesionless and cohesive soils; in layered profiles the applicable method is used in each layer, and Table 7-3 identifies methods for mixed profiles and the CPT methods. Static analyses typically estimate the pile length for a given nominal resistance to set the contract quantities; the lengths and resistance are then confirmed during construction by a field resistance determination method and a driving criterion (Chapter 17). Where static analysis alone is the resistance determination method and piles are driven to a predetermined toe elevation, the design pile lengths must address site variability. The FHWA recommended methods are the Nordlund method in cohesionless soils (7.2.1.3.1), the alpha-method in cohesive soils (7.2.1.3.2) and the API method for large diameter pipe piles (7.2.1.3.3), based on FHWA experience with their reliability for conventional pile types.
key_points: FHWA recommends Nordlund (cohesionless), alpha (cohesive) and API (large diameter pipe piles)
Static analysis sets contract lengths; a field method and driving criterion confirm them

subsections.title: Nominal Resistance of Single Piles in Soils
subsections.body: The nominal resistance of a single pile is taken as the sum of the shaft and toe resistances, Rn = Rs + Rp (p. 232). The calculation assumes the shaft and toe resistance can be determined separately and do not affect each other; many analytical and empirical methods use this approach. For typical pile sizes 18 inches and smaller in diameter or width, the nominal resistance is often calculated with the Nordlund Method in cohesionless soils (7.2.1.3.1) and the alpha-method in cohesive materials (7.2.1.3.2); piles larger than 18 inches were not in the correlation database of either method. In layered soil profiles the two methods are combined in the cohesionless and cohesive layers as applicable. Table 7-3 identifies the additional methods for mixed profiles and the commonly used CPTu and CPT methods: the API method (7.2.1.3.3), the effective stress beta-method (7.2.1.3.4), the Brown method from SPT data (7.2.1.3.5), and the Eslami and Fellenius (7.2.1.3.6) and Nottingham and Schmertmann (7.2.1.3.7) methods from CPT data.
key_points: Rn = Rs + Rp, with the shaft and toe resistance determined separately
Nordlund (cohesionless) and alpha-method (cohesive) are often used for piles 18 in. and smaller; larger piles were not in either method's correlation database
Layered profiles: combine the methods in the cohesionless and cohesive layers

subsections.title: Nordlund Method (Cohesionless Soils)
subsections.body: 7.2.1.3.1 Nordlund Method - Cohesionless Soils (pp. 232-245). The Nordlund Method (1963) is based on field observations and considers the shape of pile taper and its soil displacement in calculating the shaft resistance. It also accounts for the differences in soil-pile coefficient of friction for different pile materials, and is based on load test programs in cohesionless soils with timber, H, closed end pipe, Monotube and Raymond step taper piles, generally 10 to 20 inches wide. Large diameter open end pipe piles, concrete cylinder piles, 24 inch and greater square prestressed concrete piles and 16 and 18 inch H-pile sections are not in the calibration database; the method tends to over predict the nominal resistance for pile widths larger than 24 inches, and alternative static analysis methods should be evaluated for these pile types and sizes. The shaft resistance is a function of the friction angle of the soil, the friction angle on the sliding surface, the pile taper, the effective unit weight of the soil, the pile length, the minimum pile perimeter and the volume of soil displaced (Figure 7-8, Eq. 7-6); for a pile of uniform cross section (omega = 0) in layers of the same effective unit weight and friction angle it becomes Eq. 7-7. The soil friction angle phi influences most of the calculations; without laboratory data it can be estimated from corrected SPT N values (Section 5.2.3). Figures 7-8 to 7-14 give the design parameters, and Tables 7-6 and 7-7 give the coefficient of lateral earth pressure. Nordlund placed no limiting value on the shaft resistance but recommended that the vertical effective stress at the pile toe used for the toe resistance be limited to 3 ksf. Procedure (Steps 1-6 shaft, 7-9 toe): (1) delineate the soil profile into layers and determine phi for each (effective stress diagram, Section 7.1.4; corrected SPT N values (N1)60, Section 5.1.1; phi from Table 5-5 without laboratory or in-situ data); (2) delta from the displaced soil volume per unit length V and phi, using the delta/phi ratio for the pile type from Figure 7-9; (3) K_delta for V and the taper angle omega from Figures 7-10 to 7-13, interpolating linearly on phi and log-linearly on V between the 0.1, 1.0 and 10.0 ft3/ft curves (Tables 7-6 and 7-7 give interpolated values for uniform piles, omega = 0); (4) the correction factor C_F from Figure 7-14 with phi and delta/phi; (5) the average vertical effective stress at the midpoint of each layer (no limiting value); (6) the shaft resistance of each layer by Eq. 7-8, summed to Rs, using the 'box' area for H-piles (Section 7.10.7 for open sections); (7) alpha_t from Figure 7-16(a) for the pile length to diameter ratio and N'q from Figure 7-16(b), with phi near the toe (from SPT data, the average (N1)60 from the toe to 3 diameters below it); (8) the vertical effective stress at the toe, limited to 3 ksf; (9) Rp by Eq. 7-9, limited to qL Ap with qL from Figure 7-15, using the lesser value; for steel H and open end pipe piles the toe area (steel only, or steel and enclosed soil) is chosen from past experience and local correlations with static load tests; (10) Rn = Rs + Rp; (11) the factored resistance (Section 7.1.5, Eq. 7-3). AASHTO (2014) gives a resistance factor for this method in Table 7-1 (0.45 in sand); the factor of the field verification method, phi_dyn (Table 7-2), may also be used.

subsections.title: Alpha Method (Cohesive Soils)
subsections.body: 7.2.1.3.2 alpha-Method - Cohesive Soils (pp. 245-251). For piles in clay a total stress analysis is often used, with the nominal resistance calculated from the undrained shear strength. It assumes the shaft resistance is independent of the vertical effective stress and the unit shaft resistance is an empirical adhesion factor times the undrained shear strength. The unit shaft resistance equals the adhesion, the shear stress between the pile surface and the soil at failure (Eq. 7-10). The adhesion factor alpha depends on the nature and strength of the clay, pile dimension, method of installation and time effects; it varies within wide limits and decreases rapidly with increasing shear strength. Figure 7-17 should generally be used for adhesion, unless one of the special soil stratigraphy cases of Figure 7-18 is present; where either could be used, the inexperienced user should take the smaller value. The charts cover undrained shear strengths from about 0.5 ksf to 3.5 to 5.0 ksf, depending on the chart; users should confirm a chart's applicability with local correlations between static resistance calculations and static load tests, particularly near its limits. Figure 7-17 gives the pile adhesion Ca against su by pile type and embedded length to diameter ratio D/b, D being the lesser of the length from the ground surface to the bottom of the clay layer or to the pile toe. Figure 7-18 gives alpha against su for unique stratigraphy and embedment, used only for the adhesion of a stiff clay layer in that condition (clay layers of different consistency each get their own alpha): the top graph for piles driven through sand or sandy gravel into stiff clay (the highest alpha, falling with penetration into the clay), the middle graph for soft clay over stiff clay (alpha rising with penetration into the stiff clay), the bottom graph for stiff clay without different overlying strata (a gap forms along the upper shaft, so alpha is reduced at shallow penetration). In highly overconsolidated clays where su exceeds the upper limits of Figures 7-17 and 7-18, alpha is calculated by API Recommended Practice 2A (1993), Section 7.2.1.3.3. For H-piles in cohesive soils the shaft resistance is taken on the 'box' area: Ca on the exterior flange area plus su on the two remaining sides, approximated by the corrugated pile curve of Figure 7-17 times the box area (Section 7.10.7). In clays with large shrink-swell potential the adhesion in the shrink-swell zone is ignored. The unit toe resistance is qp = Nc su (Eq. 7-11), Nc usually taken as 9 for deep foundations. On smaller piles the toe resistance is a low percentage of the nominal resistance and is sometimes ignored; on larger piles the movement to mobilize the toe resistance is several times that for the shaft, by which the shaft resistance may have dropped to a residual value. Procedure: (1) delineate layers and determine Ca from Figure 7-17 or alpha from Figure 7-18 for each, with su, D and b (Section 7.2.1.3.3 where su exceeds the charts); (2) fs by Eq. 7-10; (3) the shaft resistance of each layer, summed to Rs; (4) qp by Eq. 7-11; (5) Rp (Section 7.10.7 for open sections); (6) Rn = Rs + Rp; (7) the factored resistance (Section 7.1.5, Eq. 7-3). AASHTO (2014) gives a resistance factor for this method in Table 7-1 (0.35); phi_dyn of the field verification method (Table 7-2) may also be used.

subsections.title: P2A (API RP2A) Method
subsections.body: 7.2.1.3.3 API Method - Mixed Soil Profiles (pp. 251-255; the heading is printed 'P2A Method'). The American Petroleum Institute static analysis procedure was developed for offshore construction, which almost exclusively uses large diameter open end steel pipe piles driven by impact hammer to final penetration (API 1993). NCHRP Report 20-05 (Brown and Thompson 2015) defines large diameter open end pipe piles as 36 inches in diameter or greater, steel pipe or concrete cylinder piles; their use on transportation projects has increased significantly. Cohesive soil: the unit shaft resistance is fs = alpha su (Eq. 7-12), alpha from psi = su/sigma'vo by Eqs. 7-13 to 7-15. An alpha of 1.0 is recommended for unconsolidated clays; for very long piles, where residual strengths are approached through extended driving and soil displacement, API (1993) recommends engineering judgment. The unit toe resistance is qp = 9 su (Eq. 7-16). The pile may be unplugged during driving but plugged under static loads; both cases should be considered in the static analysis and drivability study. Cohesionless soil: fs = K_delta sigma'vo tan(delta) (Eq. 7-17), with K_delta = 0.8 for tension and compression of unplugged open end pipe piles and 1.0 for the plugged or closed end case (API 1993); qp = sigma'vo Nq (Eq. 7-18). Table 7-8 (modified from API 1993) gives the soil-pile friction angle, limiting unit shaft resistance, Nq and limiting unit toe resistance for steel pipe piles in cohesionless siliceous soil; site exploration and testing data should be used in lieu of these guidelines where necessary. Procedure: (1) cohesive layers: average su and sigma'vo at mid-layer, alpha from su/sigma'vo by Eq. 7-13 or 7-14; cohesionless layers: delta, sigma'vo at mid-layer and K_delta from the pile type and loading direction; (2) fs by Eq. 7-12 in cohesive layers or Eq. 7-17 in cohesionless layers (with the limiting unit shaft resistance); (3) Rs by Eq. 7-4; (4) qp by Eq. 7-16 for a toe in a cohesive layer, or Nq from Table 7-8 and Eq. 7-18 in a cohesionless layer (with the limiting unit toe resistance); (5) Rp by Eq. 7-5 (Section 7.10.7 on plugging); (6) Rn = Rs + Rp; (7) the factored resistance with the factor of the field verification method. Paikowsky (2004, NCHRP Report 507) evaluated the method's reliability in cohesive soils but not in sands or mixed profiles, and AASHTO (2014) gives no resistance factor for it, so phi_dyn (Table 7-2) is used at the strength limit state.

subsections.title: Beta Method (Effective Stress)
subsections.body: 7.2.1.3.4 Effective Stress beta-Method - Mixed Soil Profiles (pp. 255-258). Static resistance in cohesionless, cohesive and layered soils can also be calculated by an effective stress method, developed to model the long term drained shear strength conditions; the effective stress friction angle phi' is used in parameter selection. The unit shaft resistance is fs = beta sigma'vo (Eq. 7-19), beta being the Bjerrum-Burland coefficient K_delta tan(delta); the unit toe resistance is qp = Nt sigma'p (Eq. 7-20). Table 7-9 gives Fellenius's (2014) recommended ranges of beta and Nt by soil type and phi'. Fellenius notes that the factors affecting beta and Nt include the soil composition (grain size distribution, angularity and mineralogical origin of the grains), the original soil density and the density due to pile installation, and the soil strength; values can deviate significantly from the table, and beta seldom exceeds 1.0. For sedimentary cohesionless deposits Nt ranges from about 30 to 120; in very dense deposits such as glacial tills it can be much higher but can also approach 30. In clays an Nt of 3 gives a toe resistance similar to a traditional undrained analysis, so a relatively low Nt is recommended in clays unless local correlations suggest higher values. Selected coefficients should be confirmed with local correlations between static resistance calculations and load tests. The method places no limiting values on the shaft or toe resistance. Procedure: (1) layers and phi' (effective stress diagram, Section 7.1.4; sigma'vo at the midpoint of each layer; phi' from laboratory or in-situ data, or for cohesionless layers from (N1)60 by a method in Section 5.2.3); (2) beta from local experience or Table 7-9; (3) fs by Eq. 7-19; (4) the shaft resistance of each layer, summed to Rs (Section 7.10.7 for open sections); (5) qp by Eq. 7-20, Nt from local experience or Table 7-9 and sigma'p at the toe; (6) Rp by Eq. 7-5; (7) Rn = Rs + Rp; (8) the factored resistance (Section 7.1.5, Eq. 7-3). AASHTO (2014) gives no resistance factor for the beta-method by Fellenius (Table 7-1: the AASHTO beta-method is based on Skempton), so phi_dyn (Table 7-2) is used at the strength limit state.

subsections.title: Brown Method (SPT N60)
subsections.body: 7.2.1.3.5 Brown Method - Mixed Soil Profiles - SPT Data (pp. 258-260). The Brown Method (2001) is a simple empirical method using SPT N60 values for the unit shaft and unit toe resistance, based on correlations with 71 static load tests from Caltrans projects in a wide variety of soil types, with closed end pipe, open end pipe, H-piles and precast concrete piles; it considers compression and uplift loading and the installation method (impact driving and partial vibratory installation). The average unit shaft resistance is fs = Fvs (Ab + Bb N60) (Eq. 7-21), with N60 taken as 50 if greater than 50 and as 3 if less than 3. Brown recommended the shaft resistance be the unit shaft resistance times the 'box' perimeter for H-piles rather than the actual pile/soil contact area, and only the external surface area for open end pipe piles. Ab, Bb and Fvs are given in Table 7-10. For impact driven piles qp = 3.55 N60 (Eq. 7-22), multiplied by 0.56 for vibratory installed piles; Rp = qp (Ap + App Fp) (Eq. 7-23), Ap being the actual steel area at the toe for H-piles and open end pipe piles. The method is recommended only for preliminary length estimates until a greater experience base exists; Caltrans continues to study and expand it (Olson and Shantz 2004). AASHTO (2014) gives no resistance factor for it, so the factor of the applicable field verification method, phi_dyn, should be used.

subsections.title: Eslami and Fellenius CPT Method
subsections.body: 7.2.1.3.6 Eslami and Fellenius Method - CPT Data (pp. 260-262). The unit shaft resistance is correlated to the average effective cone tip resistance, with a shaft correlation coefficient applied based on the soil profile: fs = Cs qE (Eq. 7-24), with the Eslami cone stress qE = qt - U2 (Eq. 7-25) and qt = qc + U2 (1 - a) (Eq. 7-26); Cs is given by soil type in Table 7-11 (after Fellenius 2014). The unit toe resistance qp = Cp qEg (Eq. 7-27) uses the geometric average of the cone tip resistance over the influence zone at the pile toe, after correction for pore pressure on the cone shoulder and for effective stress. The zone of influence depends on the pile diameter b: from 4b below to 8b above the toe when the pile is installed through a weak zone overlying a dense zone, and from 4b below to 2b above the toe when it is driven through a dense soil into a weak soil. The toe correction coefficient Cp is 1.0 in most cases; because larger piles need more movement to mobilize the toe resistance, Cp = 12/b (b in inches) for pile diameters greater than 16 inches (Eq. 7-28). Procedure: (1) obtain CPT results with cone stress and pore pressure measurements; (2) fs for each depth increment by Eq. 7-24 with Table 7-11; (3) the shaft resistance of each layer and Rs by Eq. 7-4; (4) qp by Eq. 7-27; (5) Rp by Eq. 7-5; (6) Rn = Rs + Rp; (7) the factored resistance (Section 7.1.5, Eq. 7-3). AASHTO (2014) gives no resistance factor for this method, so phi_dyn (Table 7-2) is used at the strength limit state.

subsections.title: Nottingham and Schmertmann CPT Method
subsections.body: 7.2.1.3.7 Nottingham and Schmertmann Method - CPT Data (pp. 262-268). An empirical procedure used in U.S. practice, from Nottingham and Schmertmann (1975) as summarized in FHWA-TS-78-209, 'Guidelines for Cone Penetration Test, Performance and Design' (Schmertmann 1978). In cohesionless soils the nominal shaft resistance is derived from the CPT unit sleeve friction (Eq. 7-29), Ks being the ratio of unit pile shaft resistance to unit cone sleeve friction as a function of the full penetration depth D, with the sleeve friction averaged over 0 to 8b and 8b to D. The transfer function Ks varies with total penetration (depth of embedment / pile diameter), pile material and cone type; no limit was imposed on sleeve friction in the original procedure. Without sleeve friction data, Rs = Cf sum(qc As) (Eq. 7-30), Cf from Table 7-12. In cohesive soils Rs = alpha' fs As (Eq. 7-31), alpha' being the ratio of pile shaft resistance to cone sleeve friction, patterned after Tomlinson's alpha-method, which varies with fs as shown in Figure 7-20; the method is expected to be less appropriate in sensitive soils, where the friction sleeve meets severely disturbed soil behind the cone tip. The toe resistance (Figure 7-21) uses an averaging scheme over 8 pile diameters above to as much as 3.75 diameters below the toe, favoring the lower qc values; the authors refer to a 'limit' qc of 105 to 315 ksf applied to qp unless local experience warrants higher values, and with mechanical cone soundings in cohesive soils qp is reduced by 40 percent for toe resistance effects on the base of the friction sleeve. Soil plugging (Section 7.10.7) needs careful consideration in choosing the toe area of low displacement open ended pipe and H-piles. Procedure: (1) delineate layers from qc and fs; (2) the shaft resistance of each layer: in cohesionless soils from the layer's average fs and K, with K from Figure 7-19 for the full pile penetration depth to diameter ratio (not the layer's), d being the toe depth or the depth to the bottom of the layer, whichever is less, the 'box' area for H-piles, Eq. 7-32 below a depth of 8b, and Eq. 7-30 without sleeve friction data; in cohesive soils Eq. 7-31; (3) Rs as the sum of the layers; (4) qp by Eq. 7-33; (5) Rp, using only the steel area at the toe of steel H and unfilled open end pipe piles unless there is reasonable assurance and experience that a plug will form (then the 'box' area or the full pipe area); (6) Rn = Rs + Rp; (7) the factored resistance (Section 7.1.5, Eq. 7-3). AASHTO (2014) gives a resistance factor for this method in Table 7-1 (Schmertmann 1975, 0.50); phi_dyn (Table 7-2) may also be used. Under Eq. 7-29 (p. 263) the print takes Ks from Figure 7-20; Step 2a and Eq. 7-32 take it from Figure 7-19, the sand curves.

subsections.title: Nominal Resistance of Single Piles to Rock
subsections.body: Pile foundations on rock normally carry large loads. For H-piles, pipe piles or precast concrete piles driven to rock, the area in contact with the rock, the penetration into rock and the rock quality at the contact are largely unknown, and installation can alter the rock formation (pp. 269-271). The distinction between soft and hard rock is not well defined, and the AASHTO definition for driven pile design is limited: soft rock can be penetrated by pile driving and hard rock cannot, so piles are driven into soft rock and to hard rock. In many intact rock classification systems the transition lies between unconfined compressive strengths of 200 and 1000 ksf; Kulhawy (1991) proposed 400 ksf between weak and moderate rock, and AASHTO notes that no definition of hard rock from measurable rock characteristics is widely accepted. Likins and Goble (1978) tested HP 10x42 H-piles driven to 20 blows per inch on shallow bedrock at two Ohio sites. On hard limestone (unconfined compressive strength up to 1094 ksf, at about 22 ft) static load tests reached 0.93 Fy without reaching the Davisson failure criterion (Chapter 9); on weathered shale (172 to 316 ksf, at about 15 ft) failure occurred at 0.28 to 0.71 Fy, the piles relaxed, and piles penetrating deeper into the shale had higher resistance. The study shows that geotechnical aspects control soft rock design and structural aspects control hard rock design. Tomlinson and Woodward (2015) note that piles driven to rock create very high concentrated loads under the toe; the rock's ability to carry them depends on its compressive strength, the frequency of fissures and joints, and whether they are tightly closed or open and filled with weathered material. Strong rock with closed joints or joints at a shallow angle carries very high loads, while steep open joints may give little resistance until the joints close or the rock mass locks together. Driving through weak or broken rock to hard rock can shatter the weak rock so that shaft resistance is significantly reduced or eliminated; the resulting concentrated load may suit strong intact rock but be excessive for a strong but closely jointed rock mass. Tables 7-13 and 7-14 give published and empirical nominal unit shaft and toe resistances in weak rock, for preliminary estimates or as a check of field test values, not as final design values unless the method and values are shown to apply to the site and formation. The nominal shaft and toe resistance of piles driven into or on rock is best determined from static or dynamic load tests with pile driving observations and local experience. Small diameter piles on fair to excellent quality rock are generally controlled by their nominal structural resistance (Chapter 8), since a pile on hard intact rock fails structurally before the rock; piles in soft, weakly laminated or weathered rock should be designed from static or dynamic load tests.

subsections.title: Piles Driven into Soft and Weak Rock
subsections.body: Tomlinson and Woodward (2015) note that the shaft resistance of piles driven into weak weathered rock cannot always be calculated from laboratory tests on rock cores (pp. 271-272): degradation of the weak rock, loss of shaft resistance from shattering of the rock structure by driving adjacent piles, and an enlarged hole around the pile hamper analytical methods. Axially loaded piles in soft rock should be designed with the same procedures and methods as piles in soil (the print cites Section 7.2.2; the methods for soil are in 7.2.1.3), with static and dynamic tests for design verification until local correlations and design methods are available. The empirical values in Tables 7-13 and 7-14 for H-piles in shale, sandstone and limestone were developed by Illinois DOT and give reasonable estimates of pile length and nominal resistance in that regional geology. The nominal toe resistance in soft and hard rock can also be computed by Eq. 7-34 (7.2.1.4.2), with the rock friction angle, undrained shear resistance and effective density from laboratory tests; resistances from it should be compared with static or dynamic test values and compiled in a local or regional database. Piles driven into soft rock may not need pile toe protection (a driving shoe).
key_points: Design piles in soft rock with the methods for piles in soil; verify with static and dynamic tests until local correlations exist
Compare toe resistances from Eq. 7-34 with load tests and compile a local or regional database
Piles driven into soft rock may not need toe protection

subsections.title: Piles Driven to Hard Rock
subsections.body: For piles driven to hard rock the nominal resistance is generally controlled by the structural limit state; the nominal structural resistance will generally be less than the nominal geotechnical resistance of hard rock (pp. 272-273). Where the undrained shear strength su and the rock friction angle phi can be obtained from laboratory tests on undisturbed samples of weak or hard rock, the nominal unit toe resistance qp (ksf) can be calculated by Eq. 7-34. It represents wedge failure below a foundation modified with shape factors and should not be confused with Terzaghi's equation for a spread footing; Tomlinson and Woodward (2015) added the correction factors Ps and Pt for driven pile shapes, and Nc, Nq and N_gamma come from Figure 7-22. From data of Kulhawy and Goodman (1980; 1987), qp can also be estimated from the Rock Quality Designation (RQD, Chapter 4) and the unconfined compressive strength of the rock qu: 0.33 qu for RQD of 0 to 70%, and for RQD of 70 to 100% interpolated linearly from 0.33 qu at 70% to 0.80 qu at 100%. Pile toe protection should be considered on hard rock. No static analysis resistance factor phi_stat is available for any of these rock methods, so the calculated nominal resistance should be verified during construction by a field verification method and its resistance factor phi_dyn.

subsections.title: Software for Single Pile Nominal Resistance Computations
subsections.body: FHWA previously sponsored the DRIVEN program, which used the FHWA recommended Nordlund and alpha-methods (printed pp. 274-280). The public domain version is no longer available from FHWA; a commercial version, DrivenPiles, was released in 2015. Table 7-15 lists the static analysis methods in commercially available programs (AllPile, A-Pile, DrivenPiles, FB-Deep, Unipile), alphabetically, and whether each method is in GEC-12 and in AASHTO (2014); FHWA endorses no program. An example soil profile (Figure 7-23) is analysed with DRIVEN using the FHWA method (Figure 7-24), APILE using the Nordlund and alpha methods (Figure 7-25) and UNIPILE using the beta-method (Figure 7-26). DRIVEN and APILE, though both using the FHWA method, differ by about 10% in toe and nominal resistance at the final 125 ft penetration, and at layer transitions, because APILE averages the toe resistance around layer transitions and DRIVEN does not; UNIPILE, using effective stresses in all layers, gives a lower resistance. Figure 7-27 gives APILE-FHWA nominal resistance for three pile types in the same profile: an HP 18x204 H-pile, an 18 inch O.D. closed end pipe pile and a 24 inch square prestressed concrete pile, whose displaced volume exceeds the range of Figure 7-9. The program user must fully understand a program's methodology, accuracy and limitations. Figure 7-28 is a design chart for an 18 inch closed end pipe pile: nominal resistance versus depth (APILE-FHWA) and factored resistance for different field verification methods. For a factored resistance of 1000 kips the estimated penetration is 106 ft with a resistance factor of 0.80 (static load test and dynamic tests on 2% of production piles) and 108 ft with 0.65 (dynamic tests on 2% of production piles), so a static load test may not be justified on cost there; it is 117 ft with 0.50 (wave equation analysis) and 127 ft with 0.40 (Modified Gates formula). Weighing the cost of pile length against the field verification method lets the designer choose the most appropriate method.

subsections.title: Resistance of Pile Groups in Axial Compression
subsections.body: Piles for almost all highway structures are installed in groups because of the heavy foundation loads (pp. 280-282). The nominal resistance in axial compression and the settlement of pile groups are interrelated (settlement is discussed under the service limit state; the print points to Section 7.3.2, group settlement is 7.3.5). Pile group design computations are primarily performed with computer programs such as FB-Pier or Group 6.0 rather than the simple hand calculations in the manual. The group efficiency is the ratio of the nominal resistance of the group to the sum of the nominal resistances of the individual piles (Eq. 7-35). Piles driven into relatively weak cohesive soil, or into dense cohesionless material underlain by weaker soil, may have a group resistance less than the sum of the individual resistances (efficiency below 1); in cohesionless soils the group resistance is generally greater than the sum (efficiency above 1). AASHTO gives no guidance on the efficiency of groups driven to or into rock; with equally strong material beneath, it should be 1 or greater, and groups driven into highly weathered, karst or other variable conditions should be evaluated by the designer from local conditions. The soil supporting a group is also subject to overlapping stress zones from the individual piles (Figure 7-29, a group supported by shaft resistance). Piles are typically driven into mixed soil and rock profiles; for group analysis, the stratum providing most of the nominal geotechnical resistance may be considered the controlling stratum.

subsections.title: Pile Groups in Cohesionless Soils
subsections.body: In cohesionless soils the nominal resistance of a group of driven piles at a center to center spacing of less than 3 pile diameters is greater than the sum of the individual nominal resistances, because the overlapping soil compaction zones around the piles densify the soil and increase the shaft resistance; piles at spacings greater than three average diameters generally act as individual piles (pp. 282-283). Recommendations: (1) for driven piles in cohesionless soils not underlain by a weak deposit, the nominal group resistance may be taken as the sum of the individual nominal resistances, provided jetting or predrilling was not used; jetting or predrilling can give group efficiencies less than 1 and should be avoided whenever possible and controlled by detailed specifications when necessary. (2) For a group founded in a firm bearing stratum of limited thickness underlain by a weak deposit, the nominal group resistance is the smaller of the sum of the individual nominal resistances and the resistance against block failure of an equivalent pier (the group and enclosed soil punching through the firm stratum into the weak soil). In practice block failure in cohesionless soils can only occur at center to center spacings less than 2 pile diameters, below the AASHTO (2014) minimum of 2.5 diameters; the method for cohesive soils in Section 7.2.2.3 may be used to check it. (3) Piles in groups should not be installed at center to center spacings less than 3 average diameters unless pile size, site constraints, pile cap requirements and construction costs dictate otherwise; 3 diameters optimizes the group resistance and avoids the installation problems of 2.5 diameter spacing.
key_points: Spacing below 3 diameters: group resistance greater than the sum (overlapping compaction zones); above 3 diameters piles generally act individually
Not underlain by a weak deposit: group resistance = sum of the individual resistances, provided no jetting or predrilling (which can give efficiencies below 1)
Firm stratum of limited thickness over a weak deposit: lesser of the sum and block failure of an equivalent pier punching into the weak soil (method of 7.2.2.3)

subsections.title: Pile Groups in Cohesive Soils
subsections.body: The nominal group resistance in cohesive soil is usually governed by the sum of the individual nominal resistances, with some reduction from overlapping zones of shear deformation in the surrounding soil (pp. 284-285). AASHTO (2014) states that the group resistance is influenced by whether the pile cap is in firm contact with the ground; if it is, the soil between the piles and the group act as a unit. The lesser of the group resistances from Steps 1 to 4 is used: (1) for groups in clays with undrained shear strength less than 2 ksf and the cap not in firm contact with the ground, a group efficiency of 0.65 at a center to center spacing of 2.5 average diameters and 1.0 at spacings greater than 6 diameters, with linear interpolation between; (2) clays with su less than 2 ksf and the cap in firm contact with the ground, efficiency 1.0; (3) clays with su above 2 ksf, efficiency 1.0 regardless of cap contact; (4) the group resistance against block failure by Section 7.2.2.3. (5) Piles in cohesive soils should not be installed at center to center spacings less than 3 average diameters unless pile size, site constraints, cap requirements and construction costs dictate otherwise, and not less than 3 ft. Driving pile groups in cohesive soils can generate large excess pore water pressures, giving short term (1 to 2 months after installation) group efficiencies of about 0.4 to 0.8, which increase as the pressures dissipate. Figure 7-30 shows dissipation of excess pore pressure with time for groups in cohesive soils: typically within 1 to 2 months after driving, depending on group size, but up to a year in very large groups. If a group will carry its full load shortly after construction, the designer must evaluate the reduced group resistance; piezometers should monitor pore pressure dissipation, and effective stress resistance calculations can show whether the gain in group resistance during construction meets the load support requirements.

subsections.title: Block Failure of Pile Groups
subsections.body: Block failure is generally only a design consideration for pile groups in soft cohesive soils or in cohesionless soils underlain by a weak cohesive layer (pp. 286-287). For a group in cohesive soil (Figure 7-31) the nominal resistance against block failure is given by Eq. 7-36; if the group will carry its full load shortly after construction, the remolded or reduced shear strength is used for su1 rather than the average undrained shear strength. The bearing capacity factor Nc for a rectangular group is generally 9, but for small embedment depths and/or large widths it is calculated from Eq. 7-37. For cohesionless soils underlain by a weak cohesive deposit, the weighted average unit shaft resistance of the cohesionless soils replaces su1, and the base term uses the strength of the underlying weaker layer. AASHTO (2014) Article 10.6.3.1.2d on punching failure of a footing in a strong layer over a weak layer gives additional guidance, used with the equivalent footing concept for the group.

subsections.title: Design for Axial Tension Resistance
subsections.body: Uplift resistance has become increasingly important for structures subject to seismic loading and in some cases sets the minimum pile penetration, where an axial tension load test can pay for itself through its higher resistance factor (printed p. 288; procedures in Kyfor et al. 1992 and Chapter 9). The factored uplift resistance of a single pile is the nominal shaft resistance from an AASHTO static analysis method times the uplift resistance factor phi_up (Eq. 7-38). A pile group's uplift resistance is the lesser of the sum of the individual pile resistances in tension and the resistance of the group as a block (Eqs. 7-39 to 7-41).
key_points: Single pile: Rr = phi_up Rs, shaft resistance only (Eq. 7-38)
phi_up from Table 7-1 (0.20-0.40) is 80 % of the compression shaft factor, so Rs is not reduced further
Tension static load test: phi_up up to 0.60; dynamic test with signal matching: up to 0.50

subsections.title: Axial Tension Resistance of Single Piles
subsections.body: In fine grained cohesive soils loaded undrained the shaft resistance is generally taken as equal in compression and uplift (De Nicola and Randolph 1993) (printed pp. 288-290). In free-draining soils it has been customary to take the uplift shaft resistance as about 70 % of the compression shaft resistance, and De Nicola and Randolph concluded piles have lower uplift than compression shaft resistance; API (1993) and a case reported by Altaee et al. (1992) take them as about equal. Under cyclic or sustained uplift the resistance can fall from a peak to a residual value in clays, and particle degradation can reduce it in sands (Tomlinson 1994). The factored uplift resistance is the nominal shaft resistance from any AASHTO static analysis method times phi_up from Table 7-1 (Eq. 7-38); per AASHTO Article C10.7.3.10 phi_up is 80 % of the compression shaft factor, so the shaft resistance is not reduced further. With a tension static load test an uplift resistance factor up to 0.60 may be used, and with dynamic tests with signal matching up to 0.50. Figure 7-32 is a design chart for uplift loading computed with the FHWA method (Nordlund / alpha-method) in APILE.

subsections.title: Axial Tension Resistance of Pile Groups
subsections.body: Group uplift resistance often sets the minimum pile penetration and can control the design, for example under cofferdam seals with large buoyancy forces, cantilever segmental construction, and seismic, vessel impact or debris loading, or where piles in tension are driven to a shallow bearing stratum (printed pp. 290-293). AASHTO (2014) limits the group uplift resistance to the lesser of the sum of the individual pile resistances in tension and the resistance of the group as a block; its specifications are considered relatively conservative, particularly in cohesionless soils. The factored group resistance is phi_ug Rug with phi_ug = 0.50 (Eq. 7-39). The printed contents number the two subsections that follow 7.2.3.2.1 and 7.2.3.2.2; the headings in the text, used here, number them 7.2.3.2.2 and 7.2.3.2.3.

subsections.title: Nominal Axial Resistance Changes after Pile Driving
subsections.body: The soil around a pile is greatly disturbed by driving, and as it regains strength after installation the geotechnical resistance changes with time (p. 293). Piles driven in saturated clays and loose to medium dense silts or fine sands frequently gain significant resistance after driving (soil setup). Piles driven into dense saturated fine sands, dense silts or weak laminated rocks such as shale occasionally lose resistance after driving (relaxation). Case histories of setup and relaxation are in Fellenius et al. (1989) and Thompson and Thompson (1985), respectively.
key_points: Soil setup: resistance gain after driving, frequent in saturated clays and loose to medium dense silts or fine sands
Relaxation: resistance loss after driving, occasional in dense saturated fine sands, dense silts and weak laminated rocks such as shale

subsections.title: Relaxation
subsections.body: The nominal resistance of driven piles can decrease with time after driving (relaxation) (pp. 293-294). It has been observed in dense, saturated, fine grained soils such as non-cohesive silts and fine sands, where driving is believed to make the dense soil near the toe dilate and generate negative pore pressures; these temporarily increase the effective stresses, soil strength and driving resistance, and as they dissipate the nominal resistance falls. Cases in silts and fine sands include Yang (1970), York et al. (1994), Morgano and White (2004) and Richardson (2011). Relaxation in weak laminated rocks, attributed by Thompson and Thompson (1985) to release of locked-in horizontal stresses, has been reported in shales (Thompson and Thompson 1985, Hussein et al. 1993, Morgano and White 2004) and phyllite (Seidel et al. 1992), and is possible in other weak laminated rocks such as mudstone, claystone and siltstone. Because resistance may decrease after the end of driving, static load tests or dynamic restrikes should be made after equilibrium conditions are re-established; without site specific piezometer data, testing of piles in dense silts and fine sands should be delayed a few days to a week after driving, or longer if possible, and in relaxation prone shales a minimum of ten days to two weeks. Published magnitudes are limited, but Thompson and Thompson (1985) and Hussein et al. (1993) suggest relaxation factors of 0.5 to 0.9 for piles founded in some shales (the static load test failure load divided by the nominal resistance at the end of initial driving); factors of 0.5 and 0.8 have been observed in a dense sand and an extremely dense silt. AASHTO (2014) Article 10.7.3.4.2 requires a restrike test after sufficient time for relaxation to develop where relaxation is possible at the site.
key_points: Dense saturated fine grained soils (non-cohesive silts, fine sands): dilation near the toe gives temporary negative pore pressures and a temporarily higher resistance
Weak laminated rocks (shales, phyllite; possibly mudstone, claystone, siltstone): release of locked-in horizontal stresses
Delay static tests or restrikes a few days to a week in dense silts and fine sands, and at least ten days to two weeks in relaxation prone shales
Relaxation factors of 0.5 to 0.9 in some shales; 0.5 and 0.8 observed in a dense sand and an extremely dense silt
AASHTO (2014) Article 10.7.3.4.2: restrike after sufficient time where relaxation is possible

subsections.title: Soil Setup
subsections.body: When saturated cohesive soils are compressed and disturbed by driving, large excess pore pressures develop from shearing and remolding and from radial compression as the pile displaces the soil; they reduce the effective stresses and shear strength, and so the nominal resistance during and for a time after driving (pp. 294-299). The pressures dissipate mainly by radial flow away from the pile (Randolph et al. 1979); the soil reconsolidates and gains strength, and the resulting gain in nominal resistance is soil setup. A similar loss and later gain may occur in loose to medium dense, saturated, fine grained sands or silts. The magnitude depends on soil characteristics, pile material and pile dimensions. Resistance assessments from static load tests, dynamic testing or restrikes should be made after equilibrium is re-established, which varies with soil type and disturbance; in research, piezometers within three diameters of the pile monitor dissipation, and effective stress calculations can then evaluate the gain with time. Without site specific data or local experience, static tests or dynamic restrikes in clays and other predominantly fine grained soils should be delayed two weeks after driving or longer; since such delays are rarely feasible on routine projects, setup magnitude and rate are best quantified in a design stage test program in high setup locales, with multiple restrikes on dynamic test piles and static load tests, for use in production driving where only short restrike intervals fit the schedule. In sandy silts and fine sands three to seven days is often enough. Hannigan et al. (2012) used multiple dynamic monitoring events and static load tests to quantify a nearly five-fold increase in shaft resistance on a four-level interchange. Prediction methods: Skov and Denver (1988), Eq. 7-42, for cohesive and cohesionless soils from initial driving measurements; Komurka et al. (2003) summarized the state of practice for the Wisconsin Highway Research Program; Bullock et al. (2005), Eq. 7-43, from five square prestressed concrete piles in Florida with restrikes and O-cell tests; Ng (2011), Eqs. 7-44 and 7-45, for steel HP 10x42 piles in Iowa cohesive soils (Ch from Eq. 7-44 in SI, converted for Eq. 7-45); Reddy and Stuedlein (2014), Eq. 7-46, a hyperbolic model from 76 closed end and open end steel pipe and prestressed concrete piles in the Puget Sound Lowlands with restrikes from 5 to 310 hours. These methods reflect their regional soils and pile types and may not translate elsewhere without local correlation, but suggest how agencies can build databases of initial driving, restrike and static load tests. Little is known of setup in unsaturated soils, though it is expected. Rausche et al. (1996) derived general setup factors (static load test failure load divided by end of drive wave equation resistance) by predominant soil type along the shaft from 99 test piles at 46 sites (Table 7-16); they are for preliminary estimates, setup being better estimated from restrikes, dynamic measurements, static load tests and local experience.

Delay static tests or restrikes two weeks or longer in clays and fine grained soils; three to seven days is often enough in sandy silts and fine sands
Quantify setup magnitude and rate in a design stage program with multiple restrikes and static load tests

subsections.title: Estimation of Pore Pressures During Driving
subsections.body: According to Lo and Stermac (1965), the maximum pore pressure induced by pile driving may be estimated from Eq. 7-47 (pp. 299-300). Ismael and Klym (1979) reported good agreement between measured excess pore pressures and this procedure in a case history. Poulos and Davis (1980) compiled excess pore pressure measurements from several case histories, plotting the excess pore pressure divided by the vertical effective stress against radial distance from the pile divided by the pile radius (Figure 7-35): at the pile-soil interface the excess pore pressure can approach 1.4 to 1.9 times the vertical effective stress, depending on the clay sensitivity. The designer should evaluate the potential change in nominal resistance with time; once pore pressures are measured or estimated, effective stress static resistance methods can quantify the probable change.
key_points: Delta_um = [(1 - Ko) + (Delta_u / sigma'v)m] sigma'vi (Eq. 7-47, Lo and Stermac 1965)
Excess pore pressure at the pile-soil interface can approach 1.4 to 1.9 times the vertical effective stress, depending on clay sensitivity (Figure 7-35)
Use effective stress methods with measured or estimated pore pressures to quantify the change in resistance with time
equations: Eq. 7-47: Delta_um = [(1 - Ko) + (Delta_u / sigma'v)m] sigma'vi; Delta_um maximum excess pore pressure (ksf), Ko at rest earth pressure coefficient, sigma'vi initial vertical effective stress prior to pile driving (ksf), (Delta_u / sigma'v)m maximum pore pressure ratio measured in a CU triaxial test with pore pressure measurements (Lo and Stermac 1965) (p. 299)

subsections.title: Implementation of Time Effects During Construction
subsections.body: The changes in nominal resistance after driving (relaxation and setup) are permanent physical changes (pp. 300-301). Significant cost savings can come from using soil setup effectively; as Komurka et al. (2003) note, if setup can be predicted in design it may be possible to reduce pile lengths, reduce pile sections (smaller diameter or thinner wall pipe piles, smaller H-pile sections) or reduce the driving equipment (smaller hammers and/or cranes). Relaxation has been studied less; in areas with known weathered shale or weak laminated bedrock, initial drive and restrike dynamic testing can evaluate the loss of resistance (Long and Anderson 2014), and identifying relaxation early allows modified construction procedures that avoid problem installations.
key_points: Predicted setup can allow shorter piles, lighter sections or smaller driving equipment
Where weathered shale or weak laminated bedrock is known, initial drive and restrike dynamic tests evaluate relaxation

subsections.title: Nominal Lateral Resistance
subsections.body: Piles are routinely subjected to lateral loads as well as axial compression and uplift (p. 301): vehicle acceleration and braking, wind, wave and current forces, debris loading, ice forces, vessel impact, construction procedures, thermal expansion and contraction, earth pressures on abutment walls, slope movements and seismic events. These can be of the same magnitude as the axial compression loads. AASHTO (2014) Article 10.7.3.12 addresses the nominal resistance of laterally loaded piles. For a long pile the nominal lateral resistance is controlled by the pile material, since the pile fails structurally before the soil fails along its whole length; for a short pile, one with insufficient embedment to prevent toe rotation, it is controlled by the soil. Short, rigid piles with very large lateral loads are relatively uncommon but should be evaluated in a p-y analysis considering the geomaterials and the pile's structural resistance (p-y method, Section 7.3.7.3). AASHTO (2014) notes that the strength limit state for nominal lateral resistance is in most cases only structural (Chapter 8). The deformation under lateral load must also meet the structure's performance criterion; horizontal deflection at the service limit state is in Section 7.3.7.
key_points: Lateral loads can be as large as the axial compression loads
Long piles: lateral resistance controlled by the pile material; short piles (toe rotation not prevented): controlled by the soil
Strength limit state for lateral resistance is in most cases only structural (AASHTO 2014; Chapter 8)
Short rigid piles with very large lateral loads: p-y analysis with geomaterial and structural properties (7.3.7.3)

subsections.title: Pile Length Estimates for Contract Documents
subsections.body: Pile length estimates and contract pile quantities should be established from the site subsurface information, static analysis methods and preconstruction test pile programs (pp. 301-302). Sometimes the length follows from an obvious bearing layer; otherwise construction control or static analysis may be relied on, considering the potential bias of either method, and local driving experience should be reviewed. Minimum penetration requirements for uplift, settlement, scour, lateral deflection or downdrag also enter the estimates: where the penetration for the nominal resistance in axial compression is less than that needed for these strength, service or extreme event requirements, the minimum penetration satisfying all limit states is used for the contract quantities. The contract documents should state the minimum penetration depth and the required nominal driving resistance below it, Rndr, to avoid construction control problems if the required resistance is reached above the minimum penetration. A minimum penetration is not always required; the estimated length may be all the contract documents need.
key_points: Estimate lengths from subsurface information, static analysis and test pile programs, considering method bias and local experience
Contract quantities use the minimum penetration that satisfies all limit states (uplift, settlement, scour, lateral deflection, downdrag)
State the minimum penetration and the required nominal driving resistance below it (Rndr) in the contract documents

subsections.title: Groundwater Effects and Buoyancy
subsections.body: The nominal resistance in axial compression and tension and the lateral resistance can change with the groundwater elevation through the resulting change in vertical effective stress (printed p. 302). Droughts, regional construction such as tunnels, or local excavation dewatering can lower the groundwater; a temporary lowering increases the effective stress on the pile, so a pile driven to the required nominal resistance under it will have less than the required resistance when the groundwater returns to its normal elevation. Buoyant forces should also be considered: a closed-end pipe pile driven through soft soils to rock or a hard bearing layer may need a thicker wall or other measures, since buoyancy can raise a sealed closed-end pile off the bearing layer if the shaft resistance alone cannot resist it.
key_points: A temporarily lowered water table increases effective stress: piles driven then lose resistance when it recovers
Buoyancy can lift a sealed closed-end pipe pile off its bearing layer if the shaft resistance is insufficient

subsections.title: Site Dewatering
subsections.body: Dewatering a site during construction temporarily increases the effective stresses and the soil shear strength, so piles develop more resistance at a shallower penetration and the soil resistance to reach a specified depth is greater (printed pp. 302-303); a pile type not checked for this may not be drivable to the required depth. When dewatering stops the water table rises, the effective stresses and shear strength fall, and piles driven to the nominal resistance in the dewatered condition have less than the required nominal resistance. Where significant dewatering is needed, multiple static analyses should give the nominal resistance and drivability in the short-term dewatered condition and the long-term nominal resistance afterwards. Dewatering can also increase the drag force on nearby deep foundations or cause consolidation settlement of nearby structures, which should be evaluated in design.
key_points: Dewatering raises resistance during driving and lowers it once the water table recovers
Analyse both the dewatered (driving) and the long-term condition
Check effects on adjacent structures: drag force and consolidation settlement
subsections.applicability: Driven pile sites dewatered during construction, and structures near them.

subsections.title: Artesian Conditions
subsections.body: Artesian conditions develop where a permeable layer or aquifer is confined between two impermeable layers and outcrops at an elevation higher than where it is met in-situ; the effective stresses on the pile then depend directly on the head of water (printed p. 303). They can give lower than expected nominal resistance in the layer and vertical groundwater migration along the pile-soil interface; Harris et al. (2003) describe a case where effective stress parameters back-calculated from static load tests were much lower than expected because of artesian conditions. A detailed subsurface exploration can identify them; designs whose nominal resistance needs pile lengths that punch through confining layers should be avoided, and artesian conditions should be noted on the foundation plans.

subsections.title: Scour
subsections.body: Scour is the erosion of soil and rock from the streambed and/or banks by flowing water; foundations subject to scour need input and communication among hydraulics, structures, geotechnical and construction disciplines (pp. 304-307). Scour may combine long term aggradation and degradation (streambed changes from an excess or deficit of upstream sediment), local scour at a substructure unit (clear-water, or live-bed with upstream sediment carried into the hole), and contraction scour across all or most of the channel from a flow constriction, which may be cyclic or tied to a flood. Loose granular soils can erode in a few hours of a flood; cohesive or cemented soils erode more gradually over several floods but can reach the same scour depths. Because pile resistance comes from the soil along the shaft and at the toe, scour must be evaluated in design, and multiple static analyses may be needed for the nominal resistance and minimum penetration. With local scour, the soil in the scour zone resists driving but cannot be counted on long term: its shaft resistance is included for drivability but ignored for design, while the vertical effective stress is assumed unchanged. With degradation, contraction scour and general scour, the widespread removal of streambed material reduces both the scour zone resistance and the vertical effective stress in long term calculations, which can significantly reduce shaft and toe resistance (Figure 7-36). Table 7-17 gives the HEC-18 minimum scour design and scour design check flood frequencies for each hydraulic design flood frequency. HEC-18 (Arneson et al. 2012, FHWA HIF-12-003) also recommends: reevaluating pile length, number, cross section and type for scour; designing piling for added lateral restraint and column action from the longer unsupported length (Chapter 8); recognizing that overlapping local scour holes make the scour indeterminate and possibly deeper, the top width of a local scour hole on each side of a pier being 1.0 to 2.8 times the local scour depth (2.0 recommended); analyzing the foundation with all streambed material above the total scour line removed for resistance and lateral support, though lateral stresses on the embedded pile may not be much reduced where local scour is confined near the footing; placing the top of the footing or cap below the streambed by the long term degradation plus contraction scour depth, or lower where piles could be damaged by erosion and corrosion, though in deep water a cap above the mudline may be more economical; and founding stub abutments in the embankment on piles driven below the thalweg elevation including long term degradation and contraction scour. AASHTO (2014) Article 10.7.3.6 requires scour in the minimum embedment and the required nominal driving resistance Rndr: the penetration after the design scour must still provide the required axial and lateral resistance, so piles are driven to the required nominal resistance plus the shaft resistance lost to scour, computed with the design static method (its bias considered) and excluded from the long term resistance. Restrike dynamic measurements with signal matching can determine the scour zone shaft resistance for subtraction from the nominal resistance.
key_points: Scour components: long term aggradation and degradation, local scour and contraction scour
Local scour: ignore scour zone shaft resistance for design (keep it for drivability), vertical effective stress unchanged
Degradation, contraction and general scour: reduce both the scour zone resistance and the vertical effective stress

Local scour hole top width 1.0 to 2.8 times the local scour depth on each side of a pier (2.0 recommended)
Drive to the required nominal resistance plus the shaft resistance lost to scour (AASHTO 2014 Article 10.7.3.6)
