subsections.title: Downdrag
subsections.body: Downdrag is ground settlement, or downward soil movement, relative to a pile (p. 307). Current AASHTO (2014) guidance treats downdrag and the resulting drag force as an additional load on the pile foundation, and so addresses it under the geotechnical strength limit state. That approach has generally been conservative: few transportation structures have needed corrective action for drag forces. A design procedure addressing downdrag in the geotechnical service limit state and the pile structural strength limit state is preferred; the recommended approach is presented under the service limit state in Section 7.3.6.1.
key_points: AASHTO (2014) treats drag force as an additional load at the geotechnical strength limit state, generally conservative in practice
Preferred: address downdrag at the geotechnical service limit state and the pile structural strength limit state (Section 7.3.6.1)

sections.title: Service Limit States
sections.summary: Service checks: settlement, horizontal movement, rotation, overall stability, and deformation with scour at the design flood (100-year), using Service I loads. Moulton's limiting angular distortion (Table 7-18): 0.004 multi-span, 0.005 simple-span (longitudinal only); lateral movement 1.5 in. The S-0 concept (Duncan and Tan 1991): one support may settle the computed amount while the next does not. Group settlement: elastic compression, Meyerhof SPT/CPT (cohesionless), equivalent footing (cohesive), Janbu tangent modulus, neutral plane; downdrag; p-y lateral deflection.
sections.body: 7.3 Service Limit States (p. 308). Service limit states for foundations include settlement, lateral movement, overall stability and scour at the design flood. Foundation movement should be limited to structural tolerances for both total and differential deformations; as AASHTO (2014) notes, the economics of limiting settlement, rotation and horizontal movement should be compared with the cost of designing the superstructure to tolerate the movement, including maintenance of structural or roadway elements. Deformations should be computed assuming scour will occur at the design flood. The service limit state provides limits on stress, deformation and cracking under regular service conditions; its geotechnical considerations for driven piles are vertical deformation (settlement), horizontal movements, rotation, overall stability, and deformations due to scour at the design flood (100 year event). Settlements should be determined with the Service I load combination, which includes normal operational factors only; for pile foundations in or on cohesive deposits subject to time dependent consolidation settlement, transient loads may be excluded from the settlement analysis (methods in Section 7.3.5). Load combinations for all applicable service limit states should be evaluated for horizontal movement and foundation rotation. Horizontal movement is measured at the foundation top and should be within structural limits based on column length and stiffness; sufficient geotechnical resistance and structural stiffness to resist shear and overturning loads should be checked (lateral loading in Section 7.3.7). Rotation is likewise measured at the foundation top and should be restricted. See AASHTO (2014) Articles 10.5.2.1 through 10.5.2.4 and commentary; all applicable service limit state load combinations must be evaluated. Subsections: 7.3.1 Tolerable Vertical Deformations and Angular Distortion; 7.3.2 S-0 Concept for Vertical Deformations; 7.3.3 Construction Point Concept; 7.3.4 Recommended Procedure for Vertical Deformation Analysis; 7.3.5 Pile Group Settlement; 7.3.6 Settlement Due to Downdrag; 7.3.7 Horizontal Pile Foundation Deflection; 7.3.8 Lateral Squeeze of Foundation Soil and Solutions; 7.3.9 Overall Stability.
key_points: Service limit states: settlement, lateral movement, rotation, overall stability and design flood scour
Limit total and differential movement to structural tolerances
Weigh the cost of limiting movement against designing the superstructure to tolerate it (AASHTO 2014)
Compute deformations assuming scour at the design flood (100 year event)
Settlement with the Service I load combination; transient loads may be excluded for consolidating cohesive deposits
Horizontal movement and rotation at the foundation top, within structural limits
Evaluate all applicable service load combinations (AASHTO 2014 Articles 10.5.2.1 to 10.5.2.4)

subsections.title: Tolerable Vertical Deformations and Angular Distortion
subsections.body: Tolerable deformations are limited by the structure type and function, design service life, and anticipated performance at the respective displacement levels (pp. 309-310). Vertical, horizontal and rotational displacements should be considered, with tolerable movement criteria established by empirical procedures, structural analysis, or both (AASHTO 2014). Agencies often limit vertical deformation to restrictive values such as 1 inch or less without a rational basis; there is no technical reason for arbitrary limits, but there are practical ones, such as the tolerances of attached structures and utilities, drainage, ride quality and safety. Moulton (1985) studied 314 bridges and recommended limiting angular distortions for multi-span and simple span structures. Angular distortion (Figure 7-37) is the differential settlement of the foundation, Sd, over the span length, Ls, both in the same units. Table 7-18 gives Moulton's criteria as presented in SHRP 2 Project R19B; they were developed for longitudinal movements and should not be used for the transverse direction. Moulton also recommended limiting lateral deformation to 1.5 inches for all structures.
key_points: Angular distortion = differential settlement Sd / span length Ls, same units (Figure 7-37)
Table 7-18 (Moulton 1985, 314 bridges): limiting Sd/Ls 0.004 radians for multi-span bridges, 0.005 radians for simple-span bridges
The angular distortion limits are for longitudinal movement only, not the transverse direction
Moulton recommended lateral deformation be limited to 1.5 inches for all structures
Arbitrary limits such as 1 inch or less have no technical basis; practical limits come from attached structures, utilities, drainage, ride quality and safety

subsections.title: Load Factor for Vertical Deformations
subsections.body: AASHTO (2014) includes a load factor for vertical deformation or settlement, gamma_SE, to be considered on a project-specific basis, and recommends 1.0 in lieu of project-specific information to the contrary (p. 310). The factor is used to assess force effects of settlement on the structural design, such as secondary moments within a span from settlement of a substructure support. A settlement load factor of 1.25 does not mean computed settlements should be increased by 25% to limit the probability of exceeding tolerable settlement; the factor is applied to the limit state load combinations to determine the settlement effects on the service and strength limit states. Research on further guidance for gamma_SE was in progress.
key_points: gamma_SE: AASHTO (2014) settlement load factor, 1.0 recommended absent project-specific information
It is applied to the limit state load combinations for settlement force effects (e.g. secondary moments), not as a multiplier on computed settlement

subsections.title: S-0 Concept for Vertical Deformations
subsections.body: Because subsurface conditions vary and predicted and actual deformations differ, a bridge should be designed to accommodate a realistic differential settlement and angular distortion in the longitudinal direction using the S-0 concept of Duncan and Tan (1991) (pp. 310-312). The actual settlement of a substructure unit can be as large as the value calculated by a given method, while that of the adjacent unit can be zero instead of the value calculated by the same method. The maximum differential settlement between two adjacent foundations is therefore the maximum total settlement calculated for either foundation unit supporting the span, and the maximum angular distortion is that settlement divided by the span length; these are the design differential settlement, DSd, and the design angular distortion, DA. Figure 7-38 shows the computed settlement and angular distortion for a four span bridge on two abutments and three piers; Figure 7-39 shows the design values from the S-0 concept.
key_points: S-0 concept (Duncan and Tan 1991): one support settles the full calculated amount, the adjacent support settles zero
Design differential settlement DSd = maximum total settlement calculated for either support of the span
Design angular distortion DA = DSd / span length
figures: Figure 7-38: Example settlement and angular distortion profile (after Modjeski and Masters 2015) (p. 311)
Figure 7-39: Settlement profile with design differential settlement and design angular distortion from S-0 concept (after Modjeski and Masters 2015) (p. 312)

subsections.title: Construction Point Concept
subsections.body: The settlements in Figure 7-39 assume all foundation loads are applied at once; in reality loads, and the settlements they cause, accumulate as construction progresses, so settlement and angular distortion should be evaluated separately relative to several critical points in the construction process (pp. 312-314). Figure 7-40 shows the typical construction sequence of a pier with the load applied at each stage and the resulting vertical deformation. In a typical bridge project the settlement after pier column and superstructure construction but before the wearing surface is often the most relevant; settlement before the superstructure is built may not matter to the superstructure design. Vertical deformation and angular distortion should be determined with the construction point concept in limit state designs. Figure 7-41 revisits the four span example: the calculated settlements and the S-0 maximum angular distortion, with the range of settlement and angular distortion from construction point load-deformation data shown hatched.
key_points: Evaluate settlement and angular distortion relative to key construction points, not for all loads applied at once
Settlement after pier column and superstructure construction but before the wearing surface is often the most relevant

subsections.title: Recommended Procedure for Vertical Deformation Analysis
subsections.body: Modjeski and Masters, Inc., et al. (2015), SHRP2 Report S2-R19B-RW-1, recommend the following procedure for vertical deformation (pp. 314-315). Step 1: compute the total foundation settlement at each substructure location with an appropriate method (Section 7.3.5): (a) Sta, the total settlement from all applicable loads in the Service I load combination; (b) Stp, the total settlement before the superstructure is built, from the applicable substructure loads in Service I; (c) the relevant total settlement Str = Sta - Stp. Step 2: (a) assume the relevant settlement at each support can be as large as calculated and the adjacent support settles zero, so the differential settlement Sd for a span is the larger relevant settlement of its two supports; (b) the angular distortion is Ad = Sd / Ls in radians (Figure 7-37). Step 3: the modified angular distortion Am is A times the settlement load factor gamma_SE. Step 4: check Am against owner-specified criteria, or, without them, limit angular distortion to 0.004 radians for multi-span and 0.005 radians for single span bridges; other limits may apply for vertical clearance, mitigation cost (larger foundations, realignment, ground improvement or surcharge), rideability, other structures' tolerable deformation, roadway drainage, aesthetics and safety. Step 5: evaluate the structural ramifications and modify the foundation design if necessary. The procedure is also recommended where foundations were designed for equal total settlement, because of the uncertainty of any settlement prediction.
key_points: Relevant settlement Str = Sta - Stp: Service I total settlement minus the settlement before the superstructure is built
Sd = the larger relevant settlement of a span's two supports (adjacent support assumed to settle zero); Ad = Sd / Ls
Modified angular distortion Am = gamma_SE x A, checked against owner criteria
Default limits without owner criteria: 0.004 radians multi-span, 0.005 radians single span
Also use the procedure for foundations designed for equal total settlement

subsections.title: Pile Group Settlement
subsections.body: Pile groups in and over cohesionless soils produce only immediate settlement; groups in and over cohesive soils may produce immediate settlement plus primary consolidation and secondary compression over time (pp. 316-317). In highly overconsolidated clays most settlement is immediate; in normally consolidated clays primary consolidation is generally the major source. Group settlement is likely to be many times the settlement of a single pile carrying the same load per pile, because a considerable depth of soil around and below the group is stressed, against only a small zone around and below a single pile's toe (Figure 7-42). Methods for single pile settlement are not given because piles are usually installed in groups.
key_points: Cohesionless soils: immediate settlement only; cohesive soils: immediate plus consolidation and secondary compression
A group stresses a much deeper zone than a single pile, so its settlement can be many times larger (Figure 7-42)
figures: Figure 7-42: Stress zone from single pile and pile group (after Tomlinson 1994) (p. 316)

subsections.title: Elastic Compression of Piles
subsections.body: The group settlement methods consider only soil settlement, so the elastic compression of the pile material under the axial load should be computed and added to the group settlement estimate (p. 317). It is given by Eq. 7-48. The modulus of elasticity is 29,000 ksi for steel piles; for concrete piles it varies with the concrete compression strength and is generally on the order of 4,000 ksi. The elastic compression of short piles is usually small and can often be neglected. For piles with significant shaft resistance much of the load is transferred to the soil along the pile, and Eq. 7-48 overestimates the elastic compression.
key_points: Add the pile's elastic compression (Eq. 7-48) to the soil settlement of the group
E = 29,000 ksi for steel; about 4,000 ksi for concrete
Eq. 7-48 overestimates the compression of piles with significant shaft resistance
equations: Eq. 7-48: Delta = Q L / (A E); Delta elastic compression, Q unfactored axial load (kips), L total pile length (inches), A pile cross sectional area (in2), E elastic modulus of pile material (ksi) (p. 317)

subsections.title: Group Settlement in Cohesionless Soils
subsections.body: Settlement in cohesionless soils is generally treated as elastic (pp. 317-318). Meyerhof (1976) gave elastic settlement correlations from SPT and CPT data (7.3.5.2.1 and 7.3.5.2.2), and settlement may also be estimated by the Hough (1959) method, Eq. 7-49, with the stress increase in each layer from the equivalent footing method considering the stratigraphy. Cheney and Chassie (2002) report FHWA experience that the Hough method is usually conservative and can overestimate settlement by a factor of 2, attributed to the original bearing capacity index chart being based on SPT donut hammer data. Based on the average energy differences between donut, safety and automatic hammers in the literature, Figure 7-43 now also correlates SPT N values from safety and automatic hammers with the bearing capacity index; the safety hammer values are considered N60 values.
key_points: Hough (1959), Eq. 7-49: layer settlement from the bearing capacity index C' (Figure 7-43) and the stress increase from the equivalent footing
FHWA experience: Hough's method is usually conservative and can overestimate settlement by a factor of 2 (Cheney and Chassie 2002)
Figure 7-43 includes donut, safety and automatic hammer N values; safety hammer values are taken as N60

subsections.title: Method Based on SPT Test Data

For piles in cohesionless soils underlain by cohesive deposits, the method of Section 7.3.5.3 should be used.

subsections.title: Group Settlement in Cohesive Soils
subsections.body: Terzaghi and Peck (1967) proposed evaluating pile group settlement with an equivalent footing at 1/3 D above the pile toe (Figure 7-44) (pp. 320-325). For vertical piles the footing's plan area (B)(Z) is the perimeter of the group (Figure 7-31); the load spreads within a frustum of a pyramid with side slopes at 30 degrees (drawn as 1H:2V in Figure 7-44) and causes uniform additional vertical stress at lower levels, equal to the group load over the frustum's base area at that level (Eq. 7-55). AASHTO (2014) Article 10.7.2.3.1 states that the load for group settlement is the permanently applied load. The footing depth should be adjusted to the stratigraphy and load transfer rather than fixed at 1/3 D above the toe: Figure 7-45 (Duncan and Buchignani 1976) covers a group driven through soft clay into a medium or firm layer, and Figure 7-46 covers (a) toe resistance piles in hard clay or sand over soft clay, (b) shaft resistance piles in clay, (c) shaft resistance piles in sand over clay and (d) shaft and toe resistance piles in a layered profile. Primary consolidation settlement follows from the stress increase with Eqs. 7-56 to 7-58 and the consolidation test parameters of Figure 7-47. Procedure: Step 1 (a) place the equivalent footing at the toe for toe resistance groups (Figure 7-46a) or at 2/3 D for shaft resistance groups; (b) size it to the group (Figure 7-31), or for batter piles to the group at 2/3 D (shaft) or D (toe) including the batter spread; (c) distribute the stress down to where the increase is less than 10% of the existing vertical effective stress; (d) divide the cohesive layers in that zone into layers 5 to 10 feet thick; (e) find sigma'vo and (f) the stress increase at each layer midpoint. Step 2: determine the consolidation parameters (Figure 7-47). Step 3: compute and sum each layer's settlement with Eq. 7-56, 7-57 or 7-58, and add the pile's elastic compression.

subsections.title: Time Rate of Settlement in Cohesive Soils
subsections.body: Settlement analyses in cohesive soils should also evaluate the time for the settlement to occur; the time for 90% consolidation is typically used as the total time for primary settlement (pp. 325-326). The time is calculated from Eq. 7-59 with the time factors of Table 7-19. Hv, the maximum distance water must travel from the compressible deposit to a more permeable layer, should not be confused with Ho in the settlement equations: for a cohesive layer with permeable granular layers above and below, Hv is half the layer thickness; with a permeable layer above and non-permeable rock below, Hv is the full thickness. Samtani and Nowatzki (2006) discuss the time rate of consolidation further.
key_points: Time for 90% consolidation is typically taken as the time for primary settlement
Hv = half the layer thickness when drained top and bottom; full thickness when drained one side only

subsections.title: Group Settlement in Layered Soils
subsections.body: Where piles are installed in layered cohesionless and cohesive soils, or a lower stratum of different consistency is affected by the group load, settlement depends on the stress increase in and compressibility of the affected layers (pp. 326-328). Figures 7-46(a), (c) and (d) locate the equivalent footing and the stress increase in each layer, and each layer's settlement is calculated with the equations of Section 7.3.5.2 or 7.3.5.3. Procedure: Step 1 (a) place the equivalent footing at the toe for toe resistance groups (Figure 7-46a), at 8/9 D for shaft resistance groups in sands over cohesive soils (Figure 7-46c), or at 2/3 D for shaft and toe resistance groups in layered soils (Figure 7-46d); (b) size it to the group (Figure 7-31), or for batter piles to the group at the footing depth (shaft) or at D (toe) including the batter spread; (c) distribute the stress down to where the increase is less than 10% of the existing vertical effective stress, using the permanently applied load (AASHTO 2014 Article 10.7.2.3.1); (d) divide that zone into layers 5 to 10 feet thick; (e) find sigma'vo and (f) the stress increase at each layer midpoint. Step 2: determine sigma_p, eo, Cr and Cc for each cohesive layer (Figure 7-47). Step 3: determine the bearing capacity index of each cohesionless layer from its average corrected N value and hammer type (Figure 7-43; safety hammer values are representative N60). Step 4: compute and sum the layer settlements and add the pile's elastic compression.

subsections.title: Group Settlement Using the Janbu Tangent Modulus Approach
subsections.body: The preceding methods assume a linear relation between induced stress and strain, but except at very small strains the relation is non-linear: the same stress increase causes more strain at a low original stress than at a high one (Figure 7-48) (pp. 328-334). Janbu (1963, 1965) proposed a tangent modulus approach, referenced in the Canadian Foundation Engineering Manual (1985), that expresses the stress-strain relation by a dimensionless modulus number, m, from laboratory triaxial or oedometer tests, and a stress exponent, j, generally 0.5 for cohesionless soils and 0 for cohesive soils. Strain is computed with Eqs. 7-60 to 7-66 for normally consolidated and overconsolidated, cohesionless and cohesive soils; the modulus numbers come from Eqs. 7-67 to 7-69, or for preliminary estimates from the typical, normally conservative values of Table 7-20. Procedure: Step 1 (a) place the equivalent footing at the toe for toe resistance groups (Figure 7-46a), at 8/9 D for shaft resistance groups in sands over cohesive soils (Figure 7-46c), or at 2/3 D for shaft and toe resistance groups in layered soils (Figure 7-46d); (b) size it as in Section 7.3.5.5; (c) distribute the permanently applied load down to where the stress increase is less than 10% of the existing vertical effective stress; (d) divide that zone into layers 5 to 10 feet thick; (e) find sigma'vo, (f) sigma'p and whether the layer is normally or overconsolidated, and (g) the new effective stress sigma'1 at each midpoint. Step 2: determine the modulus number and stress exponent of each layer from laboratory data (or Table 7-20 for preliminary estimates). Step 3: select each layer's strain equation. Step 4: compute each layer's settlement over its thickness Ho, sum to the 10% depth, and add the pile's elastic compression. The approach is adaptable to any soil profile.

subsections.title: Group Settlement Using the Neutral Plane Method
subsections.body: Most group settlement methods set the equivalent footing depth from an assumed load transfer; a preferred solution is to find the depth of the neutral plane and place the equivalent footing at or below it (pp. 334-336). The neutral plane is where the unfactored permanent load plus the negative shaft resistance equals the positive shaft resistance plus the toe resistance; above it the soil settles more than the pile and transfers load to it, below it the pile settles more and transfers load to the soil, so pile settlement equals soil settlement at the neutral plane and is controlled by the soil compressibility below it. The design should aim to locate the neutral plane in competent soils, which usually keeps group settlement well within acceptable limits. Procedure (adapted from Goudreault and Fellenius 1994): Step 1, determine the nominal resistance Rn from a static calculation and plot Rn minus the shaft resistance to each depth (Curve A, Figure 7-49); Step 2, plot the unfactored permanent load Qd plus the shaft resistance to each depth (Curve B); Step 3, the neutral plane is where Curves A and B intersect. It moves if the permanent load or the soil resistance with depth changes (for example preaugering, jetting or bitumen coatings), so such changes require re-evaluation. Goudreault and Fellenius (1994) note that settlement between the neutral plane and the toe is generally small because the piles reinforce the soil, and for most cases recommend calculating group settlement with the neutral plane placed at the pile toe. The load is spread below the neutral plane at 1H:2V and soils are evaluated until the stress increase is less than 10%, generally with the Janbu method (Section 7.3.5.6) or the layered soil methods (Section 7.3.5.5).

subsections.title: Settlement Due to Downdrag
subsections.body: When soil moves down relative to a pile it creates a drag force on, and within, the pile, and the potential for downward pile movement, called downdrag (pp. 336-341). The AASHTO approach treats drag force as an additional load at the geotechnical strength limit state, but drag force does not affect geotechnical strength: as the head load approaches the nominal resistance, all shaft resistance becomes positive and no drag force exists. The recommended approach (Section 7.3.6.1) is the neutral plane method of Fellenius (1989) as modified by Siegel et al. (2013), used for the structural strength and geotechnical service limit states. Drag force and downdrag always exist to some degree, from the stiffness contrast between pile and soil and from installation disturbance, so they should be evaluated in all driven pile designs: drag force in the structural strength limit state and downdrag movement in the geotechnical service limit state. The accumulation of negative shaft resistance with depth produces the drag force; a large drag force can develop in a consolidating deposit, and batter piles should be avoided where large soil settlement is expected. The maximum drag force and axial compression occur at the neutral plane. MnDOT strain gage data from a 12.75 inch concrete filled pipe pile show the neutral plane developing 30 feet above the toe (Figure 7-50); as the pile approaches the geotechnical strength limit the neutral plane moves up and the drag force reduces (Figure 7-51). Figure 7-52 illustrates soil and pile movement and the resulting forces; fill over a compressible layer (Figure 7-53) and groundwater lowering (Figure 7-54) are common causes. Briaud and Tucker (1993) listed conditions where drag force and downdrag merit careful consideration: total ground settlement over 4 inches; ground settlement after driving over 0.4 inches; embankment height over 5 feet; soft compressible layer thicker than 30 feet; water table lowered more than 10 feet; piles longer than 80 feet.

subsections.title: Recommended Approach for Downdrag
subsections.body: Siegel et al. (2013) proposed a downdrag design approach using the neutral plane method within the LRFD framework; it is the FHWA recommended method (pp. 341-348). It does not treat drag force as an additional load to be supported: drag force is a settlement consideration at the geotechnical service limit state and a structural consideration at the pile structural limit state, and it develops on all piles. The analysis needs the unfactored structural loads for the permanent load, the stratigraphy with parameters for all layers, soil load-deformation models (instrumented load tests, or t-z and q-z models), and the amount, lateral extent and timeline of fill placement. All loads and resistances should be unfactored; factored values distort load transfer and give erroneous settlement and drag force. Procedure: Step 1, assume soil consolidation and ground settlement will occur. Step 2, determine the nominal shaft, mobilized toe and total mobilized resistance versus penetration depth (Figure 7-55); shaft resistance is typically fully mobilized at 0.10 inches or less, while full toe resistance may need a toe movement of 4 to 5% of the pile diameter (Figure 7-56). Step 3, select the toe elevation. Step 4, plot the accumulated shaft resistance with depth (Figure 7-57), the unfactored permanent load plus accumulated shaft resistance (Figure 7-58), and Rn minus accumulated shaft resistance for 100%, 50% and 0% mobilized toe resistance (Figure 7-59). Step 5, read the neutral plane, the maximum axial compression load and the drag force (Figure 7-60): in the example, 100% toe mobilization puts the neutral plane at 30 feet with a maximum load of 80 tons and a drag force of 40 tons over the 40 ton permanent load, and 0% puts it at 20 feet with 60 tons and 20 tons. Step 6, check the structural strength limit state with Eq. 7-70. No AASHTO load factor for drag force from the neutral plane procedure is yet available, so local calibration is required; Minnesota DOT has adopted 1.1 while its calibration is in progress, based on an equivalent minimum factor of safety of 1.5 for material strength. Step 7, calculate the downdrag settlement with respect to the neutral plane (Eqs. 7-71 and 7-72). Later effective stress changes such as approach fill placed after driving, or changes in the permanent load or toe elevation, alter the neutral plane, maximum load, drag force and downdrag settlement.

subsections.title: Methods for Reducing Downdrag and Drag Force
subsections.body: Where the permanent load and drag force exceed the structural strength limit state, or pile settlement exceeds the geotechnical service limit state, methods of mitigating the drag force should be evaluated (pp. 348-351). (a) Increase the structural resistance: a thicker wall pipe, a heavier H-pile section of the same size, or higher strength material; a larger pile also adds surface area and so drag force. (b) Increase the number of piles, reducing the permanent load and maximum axial force per pile. (c) Reduce soil settlement by preloading before pile installation, often with prefabricated vertical drains to shorten consolidation (Rixner et al. 1986, FHWA RD 86/168; Elias et al. 2004). (d) Use lightweight fill such as geofoam (Figure 7-61), foamed concrete, wood chips, blast furnace slag or expanded shales. (e) Use a friction reducer. Bitumen coatings, applied only over the negative shaft resistance zone, have reduced negative shaft resistance by 47% to 90% in case histories; Goudreault and Fellenius (1994) suggest an upper limit of 200 psf pile-soil shear resistance in the coated zone. The coating must be protected during driving, for example by an oversized collar welded where the bitumen ends (Figure 7-62), and the bitumen chosen for the climate at installation; coatings should not be specified casually. Plastic wrap is an economical friction reducer, particularly for abutment piles driven before MSE wall construction: Tawfig (1994) found 0.006 inch polyethylene sheets reduced pile-soil shear resistance by 78% for one wrap layer (about 200 psf) to 98% for two lubricated layers (about 20 psf). (f) Prevent direct soil-pile contact with sleeves or bentonite slurry, which are generally more expensive and less effective.

subsections.title: Horizontal Pile Foundation Deflection
subsections.body: Vertical piles can be designed to withstand significant lateral loads, and modern analysis methods should be used to select the pile type and section rather than prescriptive values or added batter piles (pp. 351-353). A foundation of vertical piles only is more flexible, better at resisting dynamic loads and cheaper to build (Coduto 1994); Florida DOT often uses only vertical piles, including for ship impact (Bollman 1993). In seismic areas batter piles can deliver excessive horizontal forces to the structure, as in the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake (Hadjian et al. 1992), so lateral loads should be resisted by ductile vertical piles and batter piles avoided whenever possible. Lateral load is resisted by the pile's flexural stiffness (E and I) and by soil compression and shear as the pile deflects (Figure 7-63). Design must evaluate the nominal structural resistance and the service deflection against performance criteria, and needs coordination between the geotechnical and structural engineers. Factors: geomaterial parameters (soil or rock type and properties, groundwater, coefficient of horizontal subgrade reaction), pile parameters (shape, material and dimensions, head restraint, installation method, group action) and load parameters (static monotonic or cyclic, or dynamic; eccentricity).
key_points: Vertical piles can resist significant lateral load; avoid batter piles in seismic areas
Lateral resistance comes from pile flexural stiffness plus soil compression and shear (Figure 7-63)

subsections.title: Pile Head Fixity
subsections.body: The pile to cap connection can behave as pinned, fixed, or in between depending on the detail (Wilson et al. 2006) (pp. 353-354). A pile extending only a nominal distance into the cap behaves as pinned: restrained against translation but free to rotate. A fixed connection needs the pile embedded two to three diameters into the cap or a specially designed connection, and restrains rotation and movement in all directions. At the service limit state a pinned head typically moves more horizontally than a fixed head (Figure 7-64); at the strength limit state a fixed head generally has a larger moment at the pile head, but may or may not have larger moments below it (Figure 7-65).
key_points: Nominal embedment = pinned head; two to three diameters of embedment or a special connection = fixed head
Pinned heads deflect more at the service limit; fixed heads carry larger head moments at the strength limit

subsections.title: Lateral Design Methods
subsections.body: Lateral soil resistance of vertical piles is designed from lateral load tests or analytical methods (pp. 355-356). Lateral load tests: full scale tests during design or construction finalize or confirm the design; loading rate, cyclic versus monotonic loading and axial load should be considered in the test procedure. They may not be economical on many projects but are essential where lateral load demand controls; Chapter 9 covers procedures and interpretation. Analytical methods: two common approaches, Broms' (1964a, 1964b) hand calculation and Reese's (1984) computer solution, both treat the pile as a beam on an elastic foundation (FHWA IP-84-11). Broms' method gives lateral loads and ground surface deflections by hand but ignores axial load. Reese's p-y method, originally in COM624 and now in its proprietary successor LPILE (Isenhower and Wang 2014), models the problem more completely and outputs moment, shear, soil and pile moduli and soil resistance with depth. The p-y method should be used for all major pile foundation projects and is the FHWA recommended lateral analysis method; LPILE, FBPIER and ALLPILE are common programs, none endorsed by FHWA.

subsections.title: p-y Method
subsections.body: The p-y method, the most widely used nonlinear analysis, models soil resistance to lateral load as a series of nonlinear springs, where p is the soil resistance per unit pile length and y the lateral deflection (Figure 7-66) (pp. 356-361). Reese (1984, 1986) gave procedures for p-y curves for various soils, based on full sized instrumented pile tests and theory. The modulus of subgrade reaction is Eq. 7-73; the negative sign shows the resistance opposes deflection, and the modulus is the secant modulus of the p-y curve, constant only over a small range of deflection. Ductile curves (curve A, Figure 7-67) are typical of soft clays under static loading and of sands; brittle curves (curve B) occur in some stiff clays under dynamic loading. Curve shape depends mostly on soil properties, and also on depth, stress-strain behaviour, pile width, water table and static or cyclic loading. Table 7-21 gives representative epsilon_50 values for clays and Table 7-22 representative subgrade reaction moduli; p-y program documentation gives the curve construction procedures. The programs solve the pile-soil equations by finite differences, iterating to equilibrium and p-y compatibility in every element, and can vary flexural rigidity with moment to model cracking. For batter piles, Awoshika and Reese (1971) proposed a modifying constant of 0 to 2 on pult: 1 to 2 with the head inclined away from the load, 1 to 0 toward it; it agreed reasonably with tests on outward battered piles but less so for inward ones, so full scale tests should be considered on important projects. Output includes the generated p-y curves and deflection, slope, moment, shear, stress and soil reaction with depth (Figure 7-68). The analysis is for a single pile; extrapolating to groups and to effects of predrilling or jetting needs considerable care, and the analyst should verify that modelling assumptions (for example all elastic behaviour) hold in the results. Measured load test results should be compared with the predictions to evaluate the p-y curves (Figure 7-69).

subsections.title: Strain Wedge Method
subsections.body: p-y methods suit piles that bend and deflect; for short stiff piles, which tend to rotate rather than bend, the strain wedge (SW) method may be more realistic (Norris 1986; Ashour et al. 1998a) (pp. 362-364). A three dimensional passive soil wedge resisting the lateral load is built into the beam on elastic foundation problem, with mobilized strains in the wedge relating passive resistance to horizontal displacement (Figure 7-70); later work added multiple soil layers and pile head conditions (Ashour et al. 2002). Soil parameters are assigned to each sublayer and the wedge shape changes with them (Figure 7-71), so the springs are not modelled independently along the pile as in p-y analysis (Figure 7-72), and group effects come from overlapping wedges. The method is implemented in software such as DFSAP and has correlated well with field tests, but has not come into widespread use; many agencies continue to use p-y analyses.

subsections.title: Single Piles
subsections.body: Lateral analysis software readily analyses a single pile; the applied loads should be factored loads at the strength, service and extreme event limit states, with a geotechnical resistance factor of 1.0 per AASHTO (2014) (p. 364). Pile bents often have a single row of piles and are modelled as a single pile along the bridge alignment and as a pile group in the perpendicular direction. More often piles are in groups of two or more rows; Section 7.3.7.6 applies to both a single pile (lead row) and pile groups.
key_points: Factored loads at each limit state with a geotechnical resistance factor of 1.0 (AASHTO 2014)
Single-row bents: single pile along the alignment, pile group across it

subsections.title: Pile Groups
subsections.body: A pile group's lateral deflection is typically 2 to 3 times that of a single pile loaded to the same intensity (pp. 364-371). Trailing row piles have significantly less lateral resistance than lead row piles (Holloway et al. 1981; Brown et al. 1988) because of pile-soil-pile interaction, so laterally loaded groups have a group efficiency below 1. Brown et al. (1988) proposed a p-multiplier, Pm, applied to all p-y curves of the piles in a row by row position (Figure 7-73); in a 3 by 3 group in very dense sand at 3b spacing they found 0.8, 0.4 and 0.3 for the lead, middle and back rows. McVay et al. (1995) centrifuge tests at 3b and 5b showed Pm depends on soil density and spacing, with group efficiencies of about 0.74 at 3b and 0.93 at 5b in sand; Brown et al. (1987) found 0.7, 0.5 and 0.4 in stiff clay. Table 7-23 summarizes these and later studies; AASHTO (2014) averaged them without distinguishing soil or test type, so other Pm values may suit similar situations with lower Pm. The Brown and Bollman (1993) p-multiplier procedure is recommended. AASHTO Pm values: 0.8, 0.4 and 0.3 (third and later rows) at 3b; 1.0, 0.85 and 0.7 at 5b; interpolate between. The analyses can be run as multiple single pile p-y analyses or with group programs such as FB-Pier, FB-MultiPier or GROUP. Fayyazi et al. (2012) found that spacing within a row also matters: edge effects can overestimate group lateral resistance by as much as 30%. Procedure: Step 1, obtain the factored lateral loads. Step 2, develop single pile p-y curves from an instrumented lateral load test at the site, published correlations, or in-situ test data. Step 3, run p-y analyses with each row's Pm to get load-deflection and load-moment curves (Figure 7-74a). Step 4, average the load per pile at each deflection over all rows, and enter the group average curve with the lateral load divided by the number of piles to estimate the group deflection. Step 5, from the maximum moment versus deflection for each row (Figure 7-74b), find each row's maximum moment and stress at the group deflection and compare with the pile yield stress. Step 6, refine the evaluation considering superstructure-substructure interaction.

subsections.title: Lateral Squeeze of Foundation Soil and Solutions
subsections.body: Abutments on piles driven through soft compressible cohesive soils may tilt forward or backward with the backfill and abutment geometry: unbalanced fill loads displace the soil laterally and may bend the piles (Figure 7-76) (pp. 374-375). Stockpiles beside a pier can have the same effect. Rules of thumb: lateral squeeze and tilting can occur if Eq. 7-74 holds, and the horizontal movement can then be estimated with Eq. 7-75. Primary mitigation: (a) delay abutment piling until fill settlement has stabilized (best solution); (b) provide expansion shoes large enough for the movement; (c) use steel H-piles for high flexural tensile strength; (d) use lightweight fill to reduce driving forces.

Horizontal abutment movement about 0.25 times the vertical fill settlement (Eq. 7-75)
Best solution: install abutment piles after fill settlement has stabilized

subsections.title: Overall Stability
subsections.body: Abutments on deep foundations are subject to overall stability failure; foundation stiffness may resist the shear loading, but global stability should be evaluated if the slip surface is below the pile tips or large earth loads are generated, and to a lesser extent for walls or cut slopes on structural elements (p. 375). Per AASHTO (2014) the Service I load combination and load factor are used, and where the stabilizing system includes a structural element (deep foundation) a resistance factor of 0.65 for sliding is recommended, the inverse of the typical ASD safety factor of 1.5. Sabatini et al. (1997), Duncan and Wright (2005) and Tanyu et al. (2008) cover slope stability.
key_points: Global stability: Service I load combination; resistance factor 0.65 where a deep foundation is part of the stabilizing system (inverse of FS 1.5)

sections.title: Extreme Event Limit States
sections.summary: Extreme events (low probability; protect against collapse): check flood scour (500-year; deeper scour prism, unfactored loads, phi = 1.0 for axial compression and lateral, 0.8 or less for uplift), vessel and vehicle collision, seismic loading (liquefaction, ground movement, seismic loads and drag force; detailed seismic design in GEC-3), ice and debris, and other site-specific events; combined extreme events in 7.4.4.
sections.body: 7.4 Extreme Event Limit States (p. 376). Extreme event limit states involve events with a low probability of occurrence that can still harm the foundation and structure if not considered in design; as AASHTO (2014) notes, the extreme event limit state exists to protect against structural collapse and preserve life. AASHTO (2014) gives guidance on extreme event loading cases including ice loading and vehicle and vessel impacts; Arneson et al. (2012) details scour near bridge piers and abutments; Kavazanjian et al. (2011) discusses seismic events in depth; background on ice loads is in Montgomery et al. (1984); vessel impact design is in the AASHTO (2009) Guide Specifications and Commentary for Vessel Collision Design of Highway Bridges. Extreme event evaluations ensure structural survival of a bridge under unique major occurrences such as earthquakes, floods and vehicle or vessel collisions with return periods significantly greater than the bridge design life. Extreme event limit states for driven pile foundation design include: the check flood for scour; vessel collision; vehicle collision; seismic loading; ice and debris loading; and other site-specific situations determined by the design engineer. Subsections: 7.4.1 Extreme Event Scour During Check Flood; 7.4.2 Seismic and Seismic Induced Downdrag; 7.4.3 Ice and Collisions; 7.4.4 Combined Extreme Events.
key_points: Low probability events that can harm the foundation and structure; protect against collapse and preserve life
Return periods significantly greater than the bridge design life
Check flood for scour, vessel collision, vehicle collision, seismic loading, ice and debris loading
Other site-specific situations determined by the design engineer
References: Arneson et al. (2012) scour, Kavazanjian et al. (2011) seismic, Montgomery et al. (1984) ice, AASHTO (2009) vessel collision
sections.applicability: Extreme event limit state checks for driven piles; see the subsections.

subsections.title: Extreme Event Scour During Check Flood
subsections.body: Bridges over rivers, bodies of water and tidal areas see repeated aggradation or degradation in the scour zone, which affects foundation resistance (pp. 376-377). The check flood is an extreme event unlikely during the design life; Arneson et al. (2012) give its design requirements, with the soil in the scour zone assumed removed and providing no geotechnical resistance to lateral, axial compression or tension loads. For the applicable factored loads the piles must have adequate factored axial and lateral resistance. The check flood differs from the design flood: the 500-year check flood has a different and typically deeper scour prism; loads for structural modelling at the extreme event limit state are unfactored; and resistance factors are 1.0 for geotechnical resistance to lateral and axial compression loads and 0.8 or less for uplift. Overall stability during the check flood should be evaluated, including storm surges, tides or other floods, and debris loads. Piles should be driven deep enough to overcome the loss of shaft resistance in the scour prism. Load combinations with the check flood are in Section 7.4.4 and HEC-18; Section 7.2.9 covers scour design.
key_points: Soil in the check flood scour zone provides no geotechnical resistance (Arneson et al. 2012)
500-year check flood: different, typically deeper scour prism than the design flood
Resistance factors 1.0 for lateral and axial compression, 0.8 or less for uplift; structural modelling loads unfactored
Check overall stability and debris loads during the check flood; drive past the shaft resistance lost to scour

subsections.title: Seismic and Seismic Induced Downdrag
subsections.body: Seismic pile design issues include liquefaction effects on soil resistance, ground movements, seismic foundation loads and seismic drag forces (p. 377). Under AASHTO (2014) bridges are designed for a low probability of collapse but may suffer significant damage or disruption of service. The pseudo-static approach commonly used for many bridges is covered in 7.4.2.1 and liquefaction in 7.4.2.2; GEC-3 (Kavazanjian et al. 2011) and FHWA-NHI-15-004 (Marsh et al. 2014) should be consulted for the seismic design procedure.
key_points: Design for a low probability of collapse; damage or disruption of service may be accepted (AASHTO 2014)
Pseudo-static analysis is common; see GEC-3 and FHWA-NHI-15-004 for detailed procedures

subsections.title: AASHTO Recommendations for the Equivalent Static Seismic Force
subsections.body: Earthquake ground displacements are transmitted from the foundation to the superstructure, where the resulting accelerations generate inertial forces applied back to the foundation; the foundation must resist liquefaction effects, ground movement, drag forces and the increased superstructure loads, so the seismic loads must be determined before the required nominal geotechnical resistance (pp. 378-382). The design earthquake is the 1000 year event (AASHTO 2014), and AASHTO Article 3.10 gives the steps to the elastic seismic response coefficient Csm and the equivalent static horizontal seismic force, Eq. 7-76. Step 1: obtain PGA, Ss and S1 from the USGS seismic maps in Chapter 3 of AASHTO (2014) or the USGS design maps application. Step 2: classify the site A to F with Table 7-26 from the average shear wave velocity, SPT N-value and undrained shear strength over the upper 100 feet. Step 3: determine the site factors Fpga, Fa and Fv from Tables 7-27 to 7-29, interpolating linearly; Site Class F needs a site-specific investigation with dynamic response analysis. Step 4: build the design response spectrum (Figure 7-77) and determine Csm, by hand with Eqs. 7-77 to 7-79; Figure 7-77 shows Csm rising from As to SDS at To, constant at SDS to Ts, then SD1/Tm. The structural engineer applies Pe(x) to the superstructure by AASHTO Article 4.7.4.3; the minimum analysis depends on the seismic zone (Table 7-30), bridge regularity and operational class. In Seismic Zones 2 to 4 a liquefaction assessment is required for multispan bridges. For the Extreme Event I check the factored seismic loads are applied to the foundation for axial, lateral and overturning analysis, with resistance factors of 1.0 for axial compression and 0.8 or less for lateral and uplift (AASHTO 2014).

subsections.title: Liquefaction
subsections.body: Liquefaction is a loss of shear strength and stiffness from pore water pressure built up during cyclic loading; saturated, very loose to medium dense, fine to medium sands and non-plastic silts are most susceptible, and it has also occurred in such gravels (pp. 382-385). Where peak acceleration will exceed 0.1g, liquefaction susceptibility should be evaluated, commonly by the Seed et al. (1983) procedure (Lam and Martin 1986; AASHTO 2014 Article 10.5.4 commentary; GEC-3 Chapter 6, Kavazanjian et al. 2011). If the soils liquefy in the design event, the piles must accommodate the loss of resistance in the liquefied zone, the seismic loads, the vertical and horizontal displacements and the resulting drag force, or the liquefaction potential may be mitigated by ground improvement. Piles must penetrate the liquefiable zone and develop adequate resistance below; compression, uplift and lateral resistance during the event are evaluated with residual strengths for the liquefiable layers. Residual strengths can be approximated from SPT values (Seed 1987; Seed and Harder 1990; Olson and Stark 2002; Idriss and Boulanger 2007); Figure 7-78 gives the Idriss and Boulanger residual strength ratio sr / sigma'vo against the equivalent clean sand blow count, with N corrected for energy, overburden and fines (Table 7-31, Eq. 7-80). Kramer (2008) proposed a weighted residual strength: 20% each from Idriss (1998), Olson and Stark (2002) and Idriss and Boulanger (2007), and 40% from the Kramer-Wang hybrid model (Kramer and Wang 2007). After liquefaction the layer consolidates as pore pressures dissipate (settlement per Kavazanjian et al. 2011). Fellenius and Siegel (2008) note that liquefaction above the pre-liquefaction neutral plane has limited effect on the pile, while liquefaction below it increases the axial compression load and pile settlement; the pile must carry the increased drag force and the post-liquefaction settlement must meet the performance criteria. Lateral spread can impose large bending moments, so piles in liquefiable soils should be flexible and ductile; maximum moment is often evaluated in a p-y analysis with Reese's soft clay curve, low residual strength and high epsilon_50 in the liquefied layer. Brandenberg et al. (2007) centrifuge tests support p-multipliers of 0.05 in loose sand and 0.30 in dense sand for fully liquefied granular layers.

subsections.title: Ice and Collisions
subsections.body: Vehicle and vessel collision and ice loads are in the Extreme Event II load combination of AASHTO (2014), each treated as an independent extreme event although they often occur with other loads such as large wind loads (pp. 385-386). Because they are typically applied to the superstructure they are analysed as structural load cases and do not directly alter the geotechnical resistance as scour and earthquakes do. The Extreme Event II limit state equation is Eq. 7-81; ice, vehicle collision and vessel collision enter it as separate events.
key_points: Ice, vehicle collision and vessel collision are separate events in Extreme Event II (Eq. 7-81)
They are structural load cases and do not directly change the geotechnical resistance

subsections.title: Ice Loads
subsections.body: AASHTO (2014) covers ice loads in freshwater lakes and rivers; saltwater ice is left to specialists (p. 386). Ice forces are assumed to act directly on piers under four conditions: dynamic impact of ice sheets, static load from thermal expansion of ice sheets around piers, load from hanging dams or ice jams, and static uplift or vertical load from ice adhesion when water levels fluctuate (AASHTO 2014 Section 3.9). Dynamic ice forces depend on floe size, ice strength and thickness and pier geometry (Montgomery et al. 1984), with presumed ice crushing strengths in AASHTO (2014). Thermal expansion and hanging dam or ice jam loads are carried in the static structural analysis and produce alternative foundation load cases. For vertical forces from ice adhesion under rapid water level fluctuation, AASHTO (2014) gives Eq. 7-82 for circular piers and Eq. 7-83 for oblong piers.
key_points: Four ice conditions: dynamic sheet impact, thermal expansion, hanging dams or ice jams, adhesion uplift with water level changes
Vertical adhesion force: Eq. 7-82 circular piers, Eq. 7-83 oblong piers (AASHTO 2014)

Eq. 7-83: F = 0.2 ti^1.25 C + 80 ti^2 (0.35 + 0.03 R / ti^0.75), oblong piers; C perimeter of pier excluding half circles at the ends (feet) (p. 386)

subsections.title: Vehicle Collison
subsections.body: Vehicular collision should be evaluated where piers are within 30 feet of the roadway edge or 50 feet of a railway centerline (p. 387). Without crash protection, an equivalent 600 kip static force is applied 5 feet above grade (the print continues 'at an angle of 0 to 15 feet from the edge of pavement'), based on full scale tractor trailer tests; for wall piers a distributed load no more than 5 feet wide by 2 feet high may be applied instead if suitable for the anticipated vehicle. A barrier (embankment, guardrail or other crash protection) may redirect or absorb the collision; AASHTO (2014) requires it to be structurally independent of the pier and ground mounted, 54 inches high within 10 feet of the pier and 42 inches high beyond.

Equivalent static force 600 kips applied 5 ft above grade without crash protection
Barriers: independent of the pier, ground mounted, 54 in. high within 10 ft of the pier, 42 in. beyond

subsections.title: Vessel Collision
subsections.body: Bridges over navigable water should be designed for vessel impact; bow, deck house or mast impacts typically load the superstructure, while a head on collision with a pier should consider the full vessel mass (pp. 387-388). A design vessel of representative deadweight tonnage (DWT) is selected from the vessels passing the bridge, and the head on force is Eq. 7-84. The equivalent static force is applied as 100% parallel to the channel centerline or 50% normal to it, and both cases evaluated. Overall stability is checked with a point load at the mean high water level (Figure 7-79); all substructure components exposed to direct impact must resist the applied loads (AASHTO 2014).

subsections.title: Combined Extreme Events
subsections.body: AASHTO (2014) gives two extreme event combinations with scour: Extreme Event I with earthquake loading, and Extreme Event II with ice, vessel and vehicle collisions and hydraulic loads (p. 388). Because the check flood and the earthquake together have a low probability (Arneson et al. 2012), scour for the mean discharge or normal non-flood flow may be used in Extreme Event I. For Extreme Event II, research on the joint probability during the check flood is ongoing and judgment should be based on site-specific factors; if ice or debris jams call for a more extreme flood than the check flood, that flood may be used.
key_points: Extreme Event I (earthquake): scour for mean discharge or normal non-flood flow may be used
Extreme Event II (ice, collisions, hydraulic loads): site-specific judgment; a larger flood may govern with ice or debris jams

sections.title: Determination of Minimum Pile Penetration
sections.summary: Settlement and structure deformation must stay within tolerable limits (Section 7.3.1). After all limit state analyses, specify a minimum pile penetration only if needed; often an estimated length suffices. Per AASHTO (2014) it is the toe elevation needed for single pile and group settlement, lateral deflection, uplift, drag force from static settlement, liquefaction, axial and lateral resistance after scour, fixity for lateral loads (AASHTO is silent on how fixity is defined), and extreme event uplift and lateral loads. Check with a wave equation drivability analysis during design; if it cannot be reached, use another pile type or installation aids.
sections.body: 7.5 Determination of Minimum Pile Penetration (pp. 388-389). Foundation settlement and the resulting structure deformation should be kept within tolerable limits (Section 7.3.1). Once all limit state analyses have been performed, minimum pile penetration depths should be specified, if necessary; they may be required to limit structure vertical or lateral deformations under applied loads. A minimum penetration should be specified only if needed: in many cases an estimated length alone is satisfactory, recognizing that once piles achieve their required nominal driving resistance, driving may be terminated shorter than the estimated length. The ability of an appropriately sized hammer to drive piles to the specified minimum penetration should be evaluated during design in a wave equation drivability analysis, which checks constructability and whether the depth can be achieved; an alternative pile type or installation aids may need to be specified if it is not obtainable by conventional driving. AASHTO (2014) states that the minimum pile penetration depth shall be the pile toe elevation needed to satisfy, as applicable: (a) single pile and pile group settlement (service, Section 7.3.5); (b) lateral deflection (service, Section 7.3.7); (c) uplift (strength, Section 7.2.3); (d) penetration into soils to accommodate drag forces from static settlement stresses (service, Section 7.3.6); (e) penetration due to liquefaction (strength and extreme event, Section 7.4.2); (f) penetration for adequate axial (compression and uplift) and lateral resistance after scour (strength, Section 7.2.9; extreme event, Section 7.4.1); (g) penetration to achieve fixity for resisting applied lateral loads (strength, Section 7.2.5; service, Section 7.3.7), noting that AASHTO is silent on the definition of fixity, which varies if defined by the deflection profile, the bending moment profile or the pile head deflection; and (h) axial uplift and lateral resistance for extreme event loads (Section 7.4).

Often an estimated length suffices; driving may stop short of it once the required nominal driving resistance is reached

sections.title: Determination of Rndr to Establish Contract Driving Criteria
sections.summary: Rndr, the required nominal driving resistance, sets the driving criteria and goes in the contract with the field verification method. It adds to Rn the resistance that will be lost: scourable or liquefiable layers (unfactored) and time-dependent loss such as relaxation (divided by phi_dyn). Example (Table 7-32): Q = 200 kips, phi_dyn = 0.65, Rn = Q/phi_dyn = 308 kips (Eq. 7-85); scour 50 kips; relaxation 100/0.65 = 154 kips; Rndr = 512 kips (Eq. 7-86). A minimum penetration may also be needed.
sections.body: 7.6 Determination of Rndr to Establish Contract Driving Criteria (pp. 390-391). The required nominal driving resistance, Rndr, is used to establish the driving criteria and should be specified in the contract documents with the field method for resistance verification. It includes factors such as the axial compression loads, resistance from scourable or liquefiable layers, and time dependent soil strength changes; some conditions give a higher soil resistance at installation, so the pile should be driven to a higher nominal resistance to cover the future losses. Including Rndr with the factored load and field verification method can reduce the risk of contractor claims; a minimum penetration may also be required to satisfy uplift, lateral loading and/or serviceability. Example (Table 7-32): factored axial load Q = 200 kips in compression. Resistance lost in a scourable layer is determined by an appropriate static analysis method and is not factored (AASHTO 2014 Article 10.7.3.6): 50 kips. The pile is driven into a weathered shale that has historically lost toe resistance after initial driving; relaxation loss is factored by the verification method: an estimated 100 kips of toe resistance, which with dynamic testing and signal matching becomes 154 kips. Eqs. 7-85 and 7-86, simplified from AASHTO (2014): Rn = Q/phi_dyn = 200/0.65 = 308 kips; Rndr = Rn + Rscour + Rrelax = 308 + 50 + (100/0.65) = 512 kips. Rndr is considerably higher than the nominal resistance because of the scour and relaxation; load factors are in Table 2-3 (Chapter 2) and resistance factors in Table 7-2.

sections.title: Drivability Analysis
sections.summary: AASHTO (2014) Article 10.7.8: the engineer performs a drivability analysis during design; failure to evaluate drivability is one of the most common deficiencies in driven pile design. A pile needs the stiffness to transmit driving forces that overcome the soil resistance and the strength to withstand them. Impedance EA/C is the primary factor: a heavier H-pile section of the same size or a thicker pipe wall raises it without raising soil resistance; an inside-fitting shoe delays plugging of open pipes. Methods, in increasing cost and reliability: wave equation analysis, dynamic testing and analysis, static load tests. Particularly important for closed end steel pipe piles.
sections.body: 7.7 Drivability Analysis (pp. 391-392). Greater pile penetration depths are increasingly required to satisfy minimum penetration requirements for extreme events such as scour, vessel impact, ice and debris loading and seismic events, so the ability to drive a pile to the required depth has become more important. AASHTO (2014) Article 10.7.8 states that a drivability analysis should be performed by the engineer during the design stage. Pile drivability is the ability of a pile to be driven to the required penetration depth and/or resistance within specified material strength limits; all static analyses are meaningless if the pile cannot be driven to the required depth and nominal resistance without damage. The limit of pile drivability is the maximum soil resistance a pile can overcome at a reasonable blow count without being damaged, driven by an appropriately sized and properly operating driving system. Pile type and length, soil conditions and installation method control nominal geotechnical resistance; because type, length and method can be specified it is often erroneously assumed the pile can be installed as designed, but a pile whose drivability limit does not exceed the soil resistance to be overcome will not reach the desired penetration. The failure to adequately evaluate pile drivability is one of the most common deficiencies in driven pile design practice. Evaluation should consider soil disturbance during installation and time dependent strength changes (setup and relaxation); for economical design the soil resistance at the time of driving must be matched with the pile impedance, pile material strength and driving equipment. Subsections: 7.7.1 Factors Affecting Drivability; 7.7.2 Methods for Determining Pile Drivability; 7.7.3 Drivability versus Pile Type.

subsections.title: Factors Affecting Drivability
subsections.body: A pile must have enough stiffness to transmit driving forces large enough to overcome the soil resistance, and enough structural strength to withstand them without damage (pp. 392-393). The primary control on drivability is the pile impedance, EA/C: once the material, and so E and the wave speed C, is chosen, only a larger cross sectional area A improves drivability. A heavier H-pile section of the same size, or a thicker pipe wall, raises impedance without much change in soil resistance; an inside-fitting cutting shoe on an open end pipe delays plug formation and reduces the resistance to be overcome. Most concrete piles are solid, so a larger area usually brings more soil resistance too. Material strength has a lesser influence because it does not alter impedance, but a stronger pile tolerates higher driving stresses and may allow a larger hammer and a slightly higher resistance before refusal or damage. Other factors are the driving system (ram weight, stroke, speed and field performance) and the dynamic soil response: higher damping or soil elasticity than assumed reduces drivability (Chapters 10, 11 and 12). Predrilling, jetting and spudding can help meet penetration requirements but do not change the drivability of the section. A pile cannot be driven to a static nominal resistance as high as its structural resistance, because of the added dynamic resistance during driving; driving stress limits may cap the usable geotechnical resistance (Chapter 8).
key_points: Pile impedance EA/C is the primary control; for a given material only a larger area A improves drivability
Heavier H-pile section of the same size or thicker pipe wall: more impedance, little more soil resistance
Material strength does not change impedance but allows higher driving stresses and possibly a larger hammer
Installation aids help reach penetration but do not change the section's drivability
Static nominal resistance cannot be driven as high as the structural resistance because of dynamic resistance

subsections.title: Methods for Determining Pile Drivability
subsections.body: Three methods predict or check drivability, listed in order of increasing cost and reliability (pp. 393-395). Wave equation analysis accounts for pile impedance and calculates driving stresses and the blow count versus nominal resistance (Goble and Rausche 1986); at design stage it needs assumptions on the hammer, its performance, the drive system and the soil response, so predictions vary from field behaviour, but it is a powerful tool that should be used to check drivability, design the pile section or specify driving equipment; AASHTO (2014) calls for a wave equation drivability analysis during design (Chapter 12). Dynamic testing and analysis measure driving stresses and nominal resistance at the time of driving, and restrikes show time dependent changes; signal matching gives soil parameters for a refined wave equation analysis, but a design-stage test program is required (Chapter 10). Static load tests on test piles driven to estimated lengths are the most accurate confirmation of drivability and nominal resistance (Kyfor et al. 1992), but need a design-stage program, cost time and money, do not show driving stresses or damage, and can mislead where conditions are highly variable (Chapter 9; rapid load tests, Chapter 11). The first two methods complement static load tests, can save material and reduce delays and claims, and can reduce the number of static load tests; restrike testing shows setup or relaxation.
key_points: Wave equation analysis: drivability, driving stresses and blow count vs resistance; required during design (AASHTO 2014)
Dynamic testing: stresses and resistance during driving and restrike; needs a design-stage test program
Static load tests: most accurate confirmation, but costly, slow, silent on driving stresses, misleading in variable ground

subsections.title: Drivability versus Pile Type
subsections.body: Drivability should be checked at design stage for all driven piles, and particularly for closed end steel pipe piles, where the casing impedance may limit drivability: a thin wall chosen to save material may not develop the required resistance or penetration (example in Section 12.5.8) (p. 395). Wave equation drivability analyses should select the section and wall thickness at design stage per AASHTO (2014); an example is in Section 12.5.3. Steel H-piles, open pipe piles, prestressed concrete and timber piles are also subject to drivability limits, particularly as extreme events and larger nominal resistances require deeper penetration; long prestressed concrete piles can be limited by their tensile strength.
key_points: Check drivability at design stage for all driven piles, especially thin wall closed end pipe piles
Select section and wall thickness with a wave equation drivability analysis (AASHTO 2014)
Long prestressed concrete piles can be limited by tensile strength

sections.title: Considerations for Batter Pile Design and Construction
sections.summary: Batter piles resist large static lateral loads with less deflection, but under dynamic or seismic loading their stiffness attracts larger forces; avoid them where significant drag forces are expected. Figure 7-80 shows how batter changes group response. In group analysis (Section 7.3.7.5, after Wilson et al. 2006) the horizontal component of each batter pile's axial load adds to or subtracts from resistance; a batter pile with no vertical load acts as a vertical pile. Check conflicts with nearby facilities; avoid batter angles greater than 1H:3V.
sections.body: 7.8 Considerations for Batter Pile Design and Construction (pp. 395-397). Battered (inclined) piles are often considered where large static lateral loads are expected or structural rigidity is required; a battered pile can typically resist larger horizontal loads with less deflection than a vertical pile at the same load. Battered piles generally perform well under static loads, but under dynamic horizontal or seismic loads the stiffness benefit decreases: earthquake displacements generate load, and the added stiffness gives larger horizontal forces on the structure. Where significant drag forces are expected, battered piles should be avoided because of increased bending along the pile. Group response differs for all-vertical and mixed vertical and batter groups (Figure 7-80): in Case A a single pile rotates about a point below ground under the horizontal load and overturning moment; in Case B two vertical piles translate horizontally and displace downward; in Case C an outwardly battered lead pile with a trailing vertical pile translates horizontally and displaces upward, so batter must be considered in design. The horizontal component of a batter pile's axial load adds to or subtracts from the group's horizontal resistance depending on batter direction. Wilson et al. (2006) noted the analysis follows Section 7.3.7.5 except: (1) with a rigid cap, the vertical load at each pile head is resolved into axial load by the batter angle and its horizontal component computed; (2) the sum of horizontal components is compared with the applied horizontal load: any remainder is resisted by pile bending in a p-y analysis, and if the components are greater and opposite, the piles bend opposite to the load; (3) a batter pile receiving no vertical load from the cap has no axial load or horizontal component and behaves as a vertical pile in bending. Batter piles added to resist horizontal load are inefficient, and vertical piles could be more economical, if the batter pile receives no vertical load. Check batter angle and deviation for conflicts with adjacent foundations, cofferdams and excavation support, utilities, abandoned deep foundations, tunnels and other constraints; with an offshore lead and template, bending stresses from the hammer weight and the unsupported pile above the template add to axial driving stresses. For constructability, batter angles greater than 1H:3V should be avoided.

sections.title: Corrosion and Deterioration
sections.summary: Corrosion and deterioration of all pile types must be considered for their environment (Chapter 6, Section 6.12). AASHTO (2014) recommends, at minimum, evaluating steel corrosion, particularly in fill soils, low pH soils and marine environments; for concrete piles, sulfate, chloride and acid attack; timber piles decay from wetting and drying cycles and are attacked by marine borers and insects (AASHTO 2014 Article 10.7.5).
sections.body: 7.9 Corrosion and Deterioration (pp. 397-398; heading printed 'DETERIORATON'). Corrosion and deterioration of all pile types must be considered for the respective environmental conditions; Section 6.12 of Chapter 6 details design for aggressive subsurface environments. AASHTO (2014) recommends, at minimum, an evaluation for steel corrosion, particularly in fill soils, low pH soils and marine environments. For concrete piles, sulfate, chloride and acid attack should be evaluated. Timber piles are subject to decay from wetting and drying cycles and to attack from marine borers (printed 'marine bores') and insects. See AASHTO (2014) Article 10.7.5 and commentary.

sections.title: Additional Design and Construction Considerations
sections.summary: Minimum center-to-center pile spacing: 30 in. or 2.5 diameters (AASHTO); spacing under 3.0 diameters can cause construction difficulties and lower group resistance. Cap edge at least 9 in. from the nearest pile; pile head at least 12 in. into the cap (6 in. with embedded bars or strands). Other topics: large pile sizes, high rebound soils, soil and pile heave, piles through embankment fills, predrilling, jetting and vibratory installation, densification, and plugging of open sections, all of which affect the reliability of static analyses.
sections.body: 7.10 Additional Design and Construction Considerations (p. 398). The previous sections addressed typical geotechnical design and analysis procedures, but the designer should be aware of additional design and construction considerations that can influence the reliability of static analyses in estimating nominal resistance: the influence of time, predrilling or jetting, driving piles through embankments, soil densification, and plugging of open pile sections. Pile driving induced vibrations can also influence the final design and resistance calculations if potential vibration levels dictate changes in pile type or installation procedure. These sections fill the gaps between design and construction events that may influence long term resistance and/or construction procedures. Subsections: 7.10.1 Minimum Pile Spacing, Clearance, and Cap Embedment; 7.10.2 Identification of High Rebound Soils; 7.10.3 Soil and Pile Heave; 7.10.4 Piles Driven Through Embankment Fills; 7.10.5 Effect of Predrilling, Jetting and Vibratory Installation on Nominal Resistance; 7.10.6 Densification Effects on Nominal Resistance and Installation Conditions; 7.10.7 Plugging of Open Pile Sections.
